Katalog Berita (Halaman 50/57)

#1408. Inside Oliver Glasner's Forest struggles: Unserious players who act like superstars when they don't deserve to, alarming physical data - and squad's grumbles revealed

Published: 12:00 EDT, 2 November 2026 | Updated: 13:25 EDT, 7 November 2026

If football management were gambling, Oliver Glasner has just done the equivalent of walking into one of Nottingham’s top casinos and chucking everything on red.

Not satisfied with hammering his Forest players publicly after Saturday’s 2-0 defeat at Brentford, Glasner then had the squad running on the banks of the River Trent for their customary Sunday recovery session. The social media footage has to be seen to be believed – Premier League footballers jogging through an overgrown field, filmed by a baffled dog-walker.

Even if Forest were doing well and their players were easy to manage, these would still be risky moves. Instead, Glasner's side are 19th in the table and he is trying to handle a notoriously restless dressing room.

Forest are believed to pay Glasner more than £10million a year and until now owner Evangelos Marinakis has been patient. But in the Premier League most fans are sceptical when club officials talk about long-term projects and three-year plans. Only three of the current 20 managers have lasted three years in their current job.

Any manager who loses regularly is under pressure, particularly at a club who sacked three managers last season and another in the summer. Glasner has lost six of 10 as Forest boss and won only once. Forget the spin: results alone mean Glasner is under the pump.

If there are no signs of a reaction against Manchester City on Saturday, it promises to be an uncomfortable November international break.

If there are no signs of a Nottingham Forest reaction against Man City on Saturday, it promises to be an uncomfortable November international break for Oliver Glasner

There was not one single moment that broke Glasner’s patience but the 30th minute at Brentford on Saturday probably contributed heavily.

Forest centre back Murillo, who has regressed alarmingly this season, watched idly as Bees goalkeeper Caoimhin Kelleher launched the ball way over his head and into the path of Dango Ouattara. Ouattara then breezed past Murillo before Nikola Milenkovic turned the cross into his own net. Glasner was unhappy with the shape Murillo was in when he returned for pre-season training and was furious at such slack work.

It was not the first time Forest had been exposed like this, either. Jay Dasilva’s winner for Coventry at the City Ground in September came from a similar diagonal pass from keeper Carl Rushworth, though that time Daniel Munoz – one of Glasner’s pupils – was at fault. Again, slack. Again, sloppy.

Daily Mail Sport understands Glasner does not see enough seriousness in his squad. This group of players get on well but nonetheless, there is a view that poor results do not hurt them enough. Is it really time for laughing and joking around the training ground when you have taken one point from a possible 15?

Most of this squad have never won a European trophy, or one in Europe’s top five leagues. Glasner has three. Some around him believe there are Forest players who carry themselves like superstars when they do not deserve to.

It is thought Glasner is also frustrated with himself. Looking back, perhaps he wishes he had started with a bang, because the 52-year-old was alarmed at the physical data from previous seasons.

In 2024-25, Forest covered fewer kilometres than any other team, and last season only Liverpool and Chelsea covered fewer. In 2024-25, only Arsenal made fewer sprints; last season, only Everton were below Forest. Glasner’s Palace sides were never lower than 12th in those four categories.

When Glasner has been outspoken in the past, it has usually worked. At Wolfsburg and Frankfurt, performances improved. At Crystal Palace last season, Glasner let rip at his bosses after a game at Sunderland last January and most expected him to be sacked. Instead, he left in the summer after delivering the Conference League. The dynamic at Forest is very different though – and Glasner may soon understand why.

Glasner was unhappy with the shape Murillo (left) was in when he returned for pre-season training and was furious at the Brazilian's slack work at Brentford

Player power was a major factor in Ange Postecoglou and Sean Dyche's sackings last season. When players believe they can go above the manager’s head and vent to those in charge, they will. This is the danger for Glasner.

Daily Mail Sport understands there are players who love neither the new style – Glasner is a committed three-at-the-back man and many of the squad feel more comfortable in a back-four – nor the Austrian’s strict approach. He is very different from the avuncular Vitor Pereira, whose easy charm and light-touch approach united the squad post-Dyche and kept Forest in the top flight.

Others are surprised Glasner has not made it a priority to bring the dressing room’s strongest characters onside. Along with Morgan Gibbs-White, both Ola Aina and Callum Hudson-Odoi are powerful voices in the squad and alienating any of them is dangerous. Equally, Ibrahim Sangare and Nico Dominguez are well-respected, and both have been left on the fringes like Aina and Hudson-Odoi.

While Gibbs-White is clearly Forest’s best player, he can be a complex character. If the skipper is not 'having’ a Forest manager, his position becomes vulnerable.

It was a turbulent summer for Gibbs-White, who was frustrated no Champions League club came in for him and ultimately changed agents. He was also left out of England’s World Cup squad. Some believe that Glasner’s rigid tactical framework does not bring the best from Gibbs-White, who likes to roam across the front line and drop deep when he wishes. While Pereira understood this, Glasner does not operate like that.

At times this season, Gibbs-White’s body language has been striking. Team-mates who make mistakes feel his anger but the 26-year-old has only one goal (a penalty) and two assists this term.

Gibbs-White watched team-mate Elliot Anderson leave Forest for City last summer and perhaps questioned why he was not on the same path to the Champions League.

It is tempting to wonder about some of the advice Gibbs-White has received from those around him, though. Because if Gibbs-White is wondering why he is still playing for a bottom-half Premier League club, it is never a bad idea to look in the mirror.

Callum Hudson-Odoi is a powerful voice in the dressing room and Glasner would do well not to isolate him

If  Morgan Gibbs-White is wondering why he is still playing for a bottom-half Premier League club, it is never a bad idea to look in the mirror

Marinakis did not make Glasner the highest-paid manager in Forest’s history just to show him the door at the first sign of trouble. When the pair held talks, Glasner is thought to have stressed the need for time to make his vision work.

Neither man suffers fools and it is easy to imagine that Marinakis would have approved of parts of Glasner’s outburst. That does not give Glasner a free pass, because Marinakis factored in player feeling when dismissing Postecoglou and Dyche.

If the Glasner experiment fails, George Syrianos will come under scrutiny. Forest’s chief football officer has more power at the club than at any other time and he pushed hard for Glasner, whom he has known for some time through links to German football.

It is believed the pair had some contact over possible transfer business during Glasner’s time at Palace, and Glasner would likely have welcomed the chance to work with Syrianos at Selhurst Park.

In December 2023, Syrianos wanted Glasner to replace Steve Cooper but Marinakis chose Nuno Espirito Santo instead. Marinakis’ son, Miltiadis, is at the training ground regularly and will report back to his father. These are testing times for Glasner and his champion.

Dyche has had his say, too. During a poor run of results last season, he gathered the Forest players and staff for their views on what needed to change.

Anticipating their opinions on formations and tactics, Dyche was bewildered when one player queried the decision to move the weekly barber visit from Friday to Thursday. Nevertheless, that player is still at Forest and Dyche lasted less than four months.

Dyche  made many mistakes at Forest but his latest posts on Threads felt relevant.

If the Glasner experiment fails, George Syrianos will come under scrutiny. Forest’s chief football officer has more power at the club than ever before and he pushed hard for Glasner

The problem at Forest is that even if the players fail to stand up and be counted, they are rarely the ones to pay the ultimate price

They read: ‘The badge is bigger than all… and yet it seems not nowadays! I can only hope it turns and the culture we were insisting upon is now being assessed and realised as what was and is needed. Oliver is out there saying what I was saying… in his own style.

‘Nottingham Forest are still finding the goals hard to come by – and I had it along with my staff – we scored but nowhere near what the metrics were telling us, so not enough to stay in our job?

'We had 35 efforts at goal v Wolves and yet a 0-0 result and it culminated in myself and staff being sacked. I hope Oliver is given more time, the fans stay with him and the players stand up and be counted.'

The problem at Forest is that even if the players fail to do so, they are rarely the ones to pay the ultimate price.

#1406. Conjugation-regulated self-assembled molecules for tandem solar cells

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Nature (2026) Cite this article

Perovskite/silicon tandem solar cells on rough textured substrates are at present limited by a critical trade-off in self-assembled monolayer (SAM) design because increasing molecular conjugation enhances conductivity but often leads to unfavourable aggregation that impairs conformal coverage1,2. Here we overcome this challenge using a rationally engineered molecular spatial conjugation that incorporates tailored intramolecular distortion to suppress excess π–π stacking without sacrificing charge-transport efficiency. This steric regulation facilitates the formation of a highly ordered, conformal SAM across rough pyramidal textures. By reconciling molecular packing with interfacial coverage, the tailored interface provides optimized energy-level alignment for ultrafast charge extraction, enables improved defect passivation through adaptive conformational adjustment and acts as a robust template for high-quality perovskite film growth. Making use of this interface, the optimized tandem device achieves a notable fill factor (FF) of 85%, yielding a certified stabilized power conversion efficiency (PCE) of 35.1%. Furthermore, the device demonstrates outstanding stability, retaining more than 94% of its initial performance after 1,500 h of ageing under the ISOS-L-1 protocol. Our findings provide a clear molecular engineering route to reconcile conductivity and film uniformity while maximizing the performance of tandem photovoltaics on textured silicon substrates.

#1405. New Bromley boss Karl Robinson heaps praise on 'megastar' Jermain Defoe - with Premier League legend in talks over dugout return after walking out on Woking

Published: 08:00 EDT, 6 November 2026 | Updated: 13:33 EDT, 7 November 2026

New Bromley boss Karl Robinson has hailed Premier League 'megastar' Jermain Defoe as the ultimate professional following his abrupt departure from Woking.

Daily Mail Sport revealed on Tuesday that Defoe is in talks to join Robinson's backroom staff at League One strugglers Bromley after Andy Woodman's dismissal last month.

And while his appointment has yet to be confirmed, Robinson jumped at the chance to wax lyrical about Defoe at his inauguration on Thursday.

Bromley sit bottom of League One but their new boss believes Defoe's meticulous attention to detail would help the players find another gear.

'There's been a lot of talk but there always is with names like Jermain Defoe, who is a megastar. He's one of the greatest Premier League strikers of all time,' Robinson said.

'I have to raise and change the narrative of what this stands for,' the new boss pointed to the Bromley badge on his jumper.

Jermain Defoe is in talks to join League One strugglers Bromley as Karl Robinson's assistant

Former Salford City manager Robinson has hailed 'megastar' Defoe as the ultimate professional

'I have to bring people in to make me the best version of myself. I spoke to people who know Jermain and played with him.

'He was always first in. All the players who have played with him will tell you that. Steven Gerrard will tell you that.

'He was first in and still in the training ground at 4pm - massages, recovery, gym, video analysis of the players he's playing against.

'I was speaking to him about something completely different the other day and we were talking about discipline and professionalism.

'I said to him: "what do you do that for?". He went: "If I do everything right Monday to Friday and I play poorly, I can accept it because I've done everything in the week to be the best version of myself."

'I'm listening and I've got goose pimples on my arm. Then I'm thinking, that's probably why you're Jermain Defoe, because he did everything he possibly could to maximise his talent.

Defoe has been out of work since walking away from National League side Woking after just four months at the helm amid a strained relationship with the club's director of football.

The 44-year-old took charge of the final six games of last season and was expected to lead the club into the new campaign.

However, he failed to report for work on the eve of the season before contacting the club later that day to inform them he would not be returning.

The former England international and Tottenham Hotspur striker would add top-level experience to the dressing room, having scored 163 Premier League goals in 496 appearances - ranking 10th on the Premier League's scoring charts.

Robinson spoke as though he idolised Defoe when quizzed on his potential appointment, highlighting his humility and relentlessness as key assets to succeed as a coach.

'Failure isn't falling short, it's when you don't maximise your talent. And I think some of the players here haven't maximised their athletic, technical and tactical capabilities', Robinson added.

'For whatever reason, we need to find the key to what that is. I think someone like Jermain (would bring that) because he maximised everything he was and everything he is.

'That's almost the secret behind the genius of the top players. It's their attention to detail, professionalism and discipline – he does that over and over again.

'He's tried to manage in non-league as well. That, in itself, is dropping your ego to learn.'

Although Bromley are still working on finalising Defoe's appointment, he is expected to join Robinson in the dugout at Hayes Lane. The Ravens host Rotherham in the first round of the FA Cup this weekend as Robinson takes his first game in charge.

#1404. Everton Women Unwrap New Partnership With Nestlé Confectionery

Everton Women has announced a new multi-year partnership with Nestlé Confectionery, bringing one of the world's most recognisable food and beverage companies into the Club's growing portfolio of commercial partners.

The agreement will see Nestlé Confectionery become the 'Official Chocolate and Grab Bag Sweet Partner of Everton Women' and an 'Official Supplier of Hill Dickinson Stadium', with household favourites including KitKat, Smarties, Rowntree's, Aero, Lion, Yorkie, Milkybar and Quality Street set to feature across both venues.

At Goodison Park, Nestlé Confectionery will have a prominent presence through pitchside LED advertising, big-screen exposure and matchday activations designed to engage supporters, alongside opportunities to showcase its products at food kiosks and points of sale.

Supporters and visitors to Hill Dickinson Stadium will also be able to enjoy Nestlé Confectionery's popular range of products, extending the brand's presence across both of Everton's iconic stadiums.

The agreement represents Everton Women's second dedicated commercial partnership, following last year's deal with GGM Gastro, with further Everton Women's-focused partnerships set to be announced.

The growing interest from major businesses reflects the opportunities being created around Everton Women, with the team's move to Goodison Park offering prospective partners a unique combination of footballing heritage, an iconic stadium and access to new audiences as the women's game continues to develop.

Andrew Middleton, President of Business Operations at Everton, said:  “We are delighted to welcome Nestlé Confectionery as a partner of Everton Women and an Official Supplier of Hill Dickinson Stadium.

“Like Everton, Nestlé’s brands have been part of family life for generations, making this a natural fit for our supporters and matchday experience. Together, we will create engaging moments across both venues and bring these iconic products closer to our audiences.

“This partnership is another important step in Everton Women’s continued growth, and we look forward to working with Nestlé to bring it to life.”

Gail Stove, OOH Confectionery Lead for Nestlé UK & Ireland, said: "Nestlé Confectionery is excited to be an Official Partner of Everton Women and Official Supplier of Hill Dickinson Stadium.

"We can’t wait to share our beloved brands with visitors at these brilliant venues.

“Working collaboratively with Everton Football Club, we’ll bring the No.1 confectionery single within the leisure channel, KitKat® 4 Finger, along with other iconic Nestlé Confectionery brands for everyone to enjoy.”

Further details of Nestlé Confectionery's planned matchday activations and opportunities for Everton supporters to engage with its brands will be announced in the coming months.

#1403. Cesc Fabregas's Como win NINE-ONE in the biggest away victory in Champions League history - two weeks after thrashing Michael Carrick's Man United - in just their first year at Europe's top table

By LUKE AUGUSTUS, ASSISTANT SPORTS EDITOR and LUKE POWER, SPORTS REPORTER

Published: 17:01 EDT, 4 November 2026 | Updated: 17:59 EDT, 8 November 2026

Manchester United's 4-1 battering by Como two weeks ago now looks a lucky escape – after the Italian side romped to a 9-1 victory at Lens in the Champions League.

Cesc Fabregas' side put in a stunning performance in a record-equalling win which well and truly announced them as contenders on the biggest stage.

Como now sit fourth in the Champions League standings after also thrashing RB Leipzig and Man United, who are likely relieved that Lens took such a pounding.

It means only Paris Saint-Germain, Real Madrid, and Arsenal have got off to better starts, despite this being their maiden season in European competition.

The lakeside outfit were 3-0 up at half-time – with the scorer of the third goal, Nico Paz, paying his respects to late Tenerife striker Jesus de Miguel – before a rout after the break.

It is the latest statement win for Como, whose transformation began in 2019 when a pair of Indonesian billionaire brothers, who originally made their fortune in the tobacco industry, bought the club for $850,000 (£644,427) through their Djarum Group.

Como thrashed Lens 9-1 in a record-equalling victory in the Champions League on Wednesday

Cesc Fabregas is quickly building his name as one of the most talented coaches in Europe

With a combined net worth then estimated at $48billion (£36.4billion), Robert Budi Hartono and Michael Bambang Hartono instantly made Como the richest club in Italian football.

Rather than pursue instant success through lavish spending, Como have built steadily, investing in infrastructure, recruitment, and a clear footballing identity – and it is paying off big-time.

They have now won six games on the bounce, though they still sit fourth in Serie A five points behind leaders Lazio, who have had an almost perfect start.

Their crushing of Lens was the first time an Italian side had scored seven or more goals away from home in European Cup/Champions League history.

And their hat-trick hero on the night, Anastasios Douvikas, is now the top scorer in the Champions League ahead of Erling Haaland.

All of this comes for a side who were playing in the third tier just six seasons ago and on the back of a relatively modest summer spend of £58million on nine permanent arrivals and loanees.

'Today everything went our way,' said an ecstatic Fabregas post-match. 'A great night for Como and our fans.'

There was a poignant moment when Paz paid homage to Miguel and his hometown club, holding aloft a shirt with the picture of the late star alongside the caption: 'Rest in peace.' Though he plays for Argentina, Paz was born in Tenerife and also spent time in the club's youth system from 2014-16.

Miguel died on Tuesday morning less than 24 hours after a collision with Andorra goalkeeper Jesus Owono during their Spanish second division match on Monday. Having suffered serious head and chest injuries he subsequently suffered a cardiac arrest.

Como's Nico Paz paid tribute to Jesus de Miguel during his goalscoring celebration vs Lens

Despite playing for Argentina, Paz was born in Tenerife and also played for their youth teams

Tenerife striker De Miguel died on Tuesday morning after a horrifying clash with Jesus Owono

Como led 3-0 at half-time with hat-trick hero Douvikas scoring two at that point before Paz's goal and his De Miguel tribute.

Soon after the interval the Serie A outfit crushed any notion of the hosts coming back as they plundered in five goals in a devastating 22-minute spell which included Douvikas completing his hat-trick. Lucas Da Cunha, Marc-Oliver Kempf, Mattia Liberali, Martina Baturina also got in on the act during that period.

Ruben Aguilar pulled one back for Lens before Matteo Papaccioli rounded off the rout in stoppage time. The 18-year-old Papaccioli, who came on in the second half, is a member of Como's youth team and hasn't even played in Serie A yet.

Wednesday's win means Como have broken many records in the Champions League.

The Italian side matched the eight-goal winning margins recorded by Liverpool and Real Madrid in their 8-0 home victories over Besiktas and Malmo respectively. They also became only the second team after Bayern Munich to score nine goals in a Champions League match.

Como followed their 4-1 victory over Manchester United with another emphatic performance, becoming the first team to score nine goals away from home in the European Cup since 1971 – Feyenoord beat Olympiacos Nicosia by this scoreline – as they climbed to fourth in the standings on nine points. The previous best scoring performance by an away club in the Champions League was Bayern Munich's 8-2 win over Barcelona at a neutral venue (Lisbon) in 2020.

Fabregas's side may have made Champions League record-equalling history, but Feyenoord hold the European Cup mark for most goals scored in a single match, having beaten Icelandic side KR 12-2 in September 1969.

Lens, who suffered the heaviest defeat by a French club in the competition, are 33rd with three points.

#1402. Steely Chelsea triumph despite losing Martinez to head injury

This was the afternoon when Xabi Alonso’s Chelsea went from swashbuckling to stoic, thrilling to tenacious.

For all Alonso’s attacking vigour at the start of his reign, there can have been no more symbolically satisfying victory under the new coach than this resolute win at Everton – the most vivid example of an increasingly impressive transformation.

This was what Alonso described as “winning in a different way”. A triumph amid the adversity of losing goalkeeper Emiliano Martínez to what appears to be a serious injury after a head collision with Jarrad Branthwaite is just one facet of why the joyous visiting supporters might consider this an early turning point.

Where recently they wilted, on Saturday they thrived in securing a first Premier League clean sheet for nine months.

Much more of this and the adjectives which were splattered across Chelsea during the golden years of José Mourinho – solid, robust and dogged – will be part of the Stamford Bridge lexicon once more.

“Just one day,” Alonso warned, both acclaiming the importance of the win while wisely preaching caution. “It will be key when we manage 10 clean sheets, even though this one feels good. We need to repeat it again and again, but the mentality was very good. Sometimes it is not to play nice, it is to play good – to win second balls, and to be efficient. We needed one of these: a clean sheet and a win.”

Asked about Martinez’s condition, Alonso said: “It was a concussion, but beyond that I do not know. I have only seen one clip of the incident, so we need to wait.

“What we know is that he left the stadium conscious and is now in hospital undergoing precautionary tests.

“We need to wait. Hopefully it will not be too serious, but at the moment we just have to wait.”

Alonso is speedily shifting perceptions of this previously underperforming bunch, the Stamford Bridge culture on and off the pitch already unrecognisable from a few months ago.

It was Chelsea’s trip to Everton last season which facilitated the endgame of Liam Rosenior’s short, but generally hideous reign.

For those who tried to banish memories, it was a darkly comical period when Chelsea’s players were paying their respect to stationary footballs, seemingly finding new ways to stand in front of travelling fans to apologise for meek and rancid performances.

How different the scenes after Pedro Neto’s double on Merseyside – a success built on those old-fashioned and too often underestimated qualities of character and application before the artists had the final say. These are the wins that build connections and trust between players and supporters, especially during the getting-to-know-you period of a managerial tenure. While neutrals mutter about a generally disappointing spectacle, the players and supporters return home clutching three points believing they have fought together in the trenches.

Neto fires past Pickford to double Chelsea's lead! 🔥 Watch live on TNT Sports and HBO Max 📺 https://t.co/fRCRh6tXYB https://t.co/SOJeBP5mq0

It cannot be overlooked how this win owed a debt to the erratic refereeing of Paul Tierney, especially the amnesty he offered to Morgan Rogers on the stroke of half-time.

Already booked, Rogers was fortunate not to receive a second caution for a lunge on James Garner which took the man after the ball. A replica challenge by Everton’s Harrison Armstrong had warranted a yellow card in Tierney’s world just 21 minutes earlier.

The home team’s argument that this was a potential game changer was supported when the England midfielder was inevitably involved in the move which led to Neto breaking through 44 seconds into the second half – a lead Chelsea never looked like surrendering as Everton’s attacking limitations were exposed.

Chelsea break the deadlock inside a minute of the second half! ⚡ Watch live on TNT Sports and HBO Max 📺 https://t.co/fRCRh6tXYB https://t.co/E63rtGQnbv

That should not disguise how this is a different Chelsea, contrasting not just with the characterless and rudderless team of last season, but also the defensively flawed version that began this one. Mike Penders deputised for the stricken Martínez – conscious but taken to hospital as a precaution – and was well-protected.

As much as Alonso’s artistry as a midfield maestro is presumed to define him as a coach, one cannot help but believe there are many who underestimate him as a football student. He was never going to return to England clinging to one idea given his previous Premier League experience, and he intuitively knew an away game at Everton was one for foot soldiers.

He signed Jordan Henderson for such a task. Just like his manager, the former Liverpool captain was primed for enemy territory.

Alonso’s anticipation of a fixture in which a battle had to be fought before there was an outbreak of football proved correct, aided by the fussy and generally terrible first-half officiating of Tierney.

Bizarrely, Alonso had as much cause to curse Tierney for the first of several contentious decisions, booking Armstrong for an aggressive but ultimately fair lunging challenge on Josh Acheampong. That enraged the home supporters to inspire Everton to their most dangerous spell, Thierno Barry coming closest to troubling Martínez before half-time.

Although Moisés Caicedo was denied a goal-of-the-season contender when a vicious 20-yard volley struck the crossbar, the scrappy, stop-start flavour of the occasion initially suited the hosts.

Caicedo rattles the woodwork with a stunning effort! 💥 Watch live on TNT Sports and HBO Max 📺 https://t.co/fRCRh6tXYB https://t.co/CSIM9ogtSp

Rogers’s reprieve changed all that. Inexplicably inconsistent as Tierney was, Chelsea exhibited a steel which thrilled Alonso as much as those games when Cole Palmer, Rogers and João Pedro are in full flow.

“They didn’t score, but did a fantastic job for the team,” Alonso pointedly said of his attackers.

Alonso’s name has not echoed so loudly across the Mersey since he played a few miles down the road from Everton’s new home. After several calamitous appointments, those fans can believe their team are in safe hands again.

A good win for Chelsea at Everton, but above all, let’s hope Martinez is back to full health soon.

Moyes accepted that his side had were not good enough.

He told TNT Sports: “We were a little bit unlucky with the goals. It wasn’t good defending, but it takes a couple of deflections before it gets to Neto. It makes it a relatively easy finish for him.

“The second one was a free-kick which obviously ricochets around, so I think there were parts of the game we did OK, but we didn’t offer enough to create enough, to make enough chances. I can’t think of many, so that is probably the biggest indictment.”

He had a minor gripe over a first-half tackle that was reviewed, saying, “I think the Morgan Rogers tackle on Jimmy [Garner] could have been questioned.”

However, given the good start to the season for Everton so far, he does not have too much rancour.

"Not as good as we wanted." 💬 David Moyes reflects on Everton's defeat to Chelsea 🔵 🎙️ @jules_breach | Watch live on TNT Sports and HBO Max 📺 https://t.co/fRCRh6tXYB https://t.co/qPU64VjHYC

Speaking to TNT Sports after the match, Xabi Alonso gives relatively positive news on Emi Martinez.

He describes the planned tests as “precautionary” and says, “as far as I know, he left the stadium conscious.”

Neto added more detail to his thoughts on the game.

On his first goal, he explained how Everton’s defensive approach allowed them to react: “We know that they came man-to man. In the second half we adjusted some stuff. We tried to get the best of the man-to-man press and we got away. We got the cross and I could finish well, so really happy.”

He credited his Portugal coach, Jorge Jesus, with his calmness in front of goal, adding: “This comes a little bit from the new coach of the national team that says when you are near to the area you need to pass to the goal, so really happy with that.”

With Chelsea now in the Champions League places, Neto was keen to keep up the momentum. He said: “It’s really important. We know it’s tough to play away, even at home there are no easy games. We came here with personality, with good intentions to win the match and really happy with the result.”

An eventful match without too many chances.

Jordan Pickford and Emi Martinez have both been alert to danger, but the match is mainly fraying at the edges. Fouls and tempers are the story, with a subtext of bookings creeping up.

Armstrong clears a flick-on off the line for the third corner.  Chelsea put the pressure on, but Everton clear for now.

Pickford pushes a Neto shot over the bar. Mykolenko nodes behind for another corner at the near post, and then again for the next set piece.

The Chelsea players continue to complain. Garner needs to go off as he received treatment, but Rogers remains on.

A poor clearance from Martinez puts Chelsea in trouble, but Rogers closes him down to put it out of play. Armstrong goes down. Moments later, Rogers and Garner go in hard on a 50-50, and there is yet more complaining from the players. Both players’ studs connected with the other, it seems.

This could go south for one or both of them, depending on how the ref sees it, but the check clears them both.

Caicedo hits the post! Henderson picks out Caicedo with a brilliant corner, and the midfielder strikes it on the volley, smashing it against the woodwork.

Barry spins and shoots after Mykolenko dashes into the box and lays the ball off.

Martinez saves comfortably, and Barry goes down, needing treatment.

The game has stretched out now, and with a few players on yellow - five in total - it is harder for them to stick a foot in.

I’m getting the feeling that referee Tierney took a long look in the mirror this morning, stiffened his back and boldly declared, “Today, I am the main man.”

To describe his officiating so far as erratic is an understatement. But it has brought the stadium to life, so maybe we should thank him.

Acheampong sticks a leg out and catches Grealish as he bursts forward, and gets a booking. An early moment of contact in the box between Pedro and Tarkowski is reviewed, and it is waved away.

Moments later, tempers fray as Henderson objects to a foul, I think from Tarkowski, and they all come together for a shoving. Rogers and Tarkowski are booked as the Everton defender barged into the Rogers off the ball.

Everton have had 31% of the ball, but they’re coming back into it. A set piece works the ball to Grealish from Dewsbury-Hall, and he volleys into the ground that Martinez tips away. Everton build patiently from the corner, but Grealish is tackled on the left wing.

A booking for Armstrong for what those of a certain age will consider an aggressive, on-the-edge, but ultimately fair tackle, qualifies as today’s first “the game has gone” moment.

A shot of note. A wild moment. Rohl skids into the box and digs out a shot from inside the box, but it’s hardly magical and it’s easily stopped.

Martinez concedes a corner by holding onto the ball for too long, and Neto gets booked for dissent. An awful corner, and it’s cleared, but Grealish picks the ball and delivers for Barry, who glances his effort straight at Martinez. A decent spell for Everton.

Palmer boots the ball into the air in frustration after a decision goes against him, and he escapes a booking. I mean, it’s hardly a great offence, but now Everton fans will be alert to anything similar that might go against him.

Armstrong then does go into the book for a strong tackle on Acheampong, with both sides up in arms over the decision.

He took the ball, and the man, but while it was fairly meaty, it wasn’t dirty.

Colwill and Barry collide off the ball but there are no afters, Chelsea keep looking.

Neto pulls the ball back for Neto a few moments later, but his low shot is blocked, and Chelsea push forward again.

Corner on the right wing for Everton. Dewsbury-Hall’s cross is cleared at the near post. Grealish sends it back in, but it is overhit and drifts out of play. Chris Bascombe observes the stop-start nature of the game.

Referee Paul Tierney appears to be in one of those moods where if anyone falls over near an opponent, he’ll give a foul. It’s making for a scrappy game, which is suiting Everton.

A shot! Palmer lines up a shot from 25 yards, onto his left foot. It bounces in front of Pickford, who holds well. Pickford has five goals in seven appearances against Everton, so he probably fancies his chances.

Caicedo is crowded out by Dewsbury-Hall, and the Chelsea man almost goes into the book for his efforts. Given his early fouls and arguments, he may be walking on thin ice.

Everton playing like a completely Moyes side. At their best, they are dangerous on the counter and solid at the back. When it goes wrong, the lack of creativity hurts Moyes’ sides, but right now they are holding their own.

Given the jeering for Henderson from the Evertonians, they clearly have not softened their stance on his Anfield past after seeing him tapping the Chelsea badge last weekend. A few Liverpool supporters watching might share their sentiments.

Pedro appears to have taken a clump to the gob, and has a mouthful of tissue or bandage to stem the flow. He remains on the pitch, though.

Grealish plucks a Chelsea crossfield ball out of the air as if he was smoking a cigarette rolled by Dimitar Berbatov as he listened to Ornette Coleman. Sadly after that, his pass out to the right wing went nowhere.

Grealish chases a ball over the top and wins a throw on the left wing. The Everton fans are in decent voice. Mykolenko launches a long throw into the box, but it’s cleared for now.

Grealish and Caiceido get up in each others’ grills, but it settles down.

Chelsea keep the ball for most of the early stages, but Caicedo concedes a foul in midfield.

Chelsea captain Reece James’ surgery could be out for a couple of months, Xabi Alonso explained.

He told the  press: “I wish him the best recovery. We won’t set timelines, but we expect him to be out for several weeks. It’s not going to be short. Whether it’s before or after Christmas then time will tell. It needs to be done properly.”

He is looking to vice captains Moises Caceido and Levi Colwill to step up in his absence, explaining: “You can be a captain without an armband, for sure. Leadership is important and that’s why we have this group, not just on matchday.”

James remains vital to Chelsea at their best, and while his minutes have been managed, it’s a huge disappointment to see him need to go under the knife once more.

In his press conference ahead of the weekend, Everton boss David Moyes was not too concerned by his relatively small squad.He said:  “Leicester City won the league with not too many players. We have not got too many players. I am not saying we’re going to win the league, but we want to try to challenge and be around the top teams.”

That might be made harder by the news that the Friedkin Group are already looking to sell the club after only a couple of years in charge. Moyes is a rare thing, a manager who keeps improving despite setbacks, and his second spell has been fairly solid so far.

Moyes is aware that Chelsea pose a threat up front, adding: “Their attacking line is incredibly exciting. I also think they have got some super defenders as well, but they are playing quite an expansive game, which on its day can lead to goals and on another day it can lead to defeats.”

Welcome to Telegraph Sport’s live coverage of Everton vs Chelsea.

Chelsea return to Premier League action this weekend looking to harness the momentum of their emphatic 5-1 victory over Bournemouth before the international break. That Stamford Bridge masterclass ended a frustrating three-match winless streak and was built upon braces from Joao Pedro and Jordan Henderson, alongside another strike from summer signing Morgan Rogers.

Yet the true catalyst for the resurgence was the return of Moises Caicedo. Having shaken off the calf problem that hindered his early-season involvement, the midfielder anchored the side’s win. While defensive vulnerabilities persist - extending an unwanted run of league matches without a clean sheet back to January - the victory offered clear signs of progress under their head coach, Xabi Alonso.

Next up is a notoriously difficult trip to Merseyside to face Everton in Saturday’s lunchtime fixture. Historically, Everton have proven to be a formidable stumbling block for the capital club, particularly on home turf. Everton enter the weekend unbeaten in eight of their last nine home encounters against Chelsea, a stretch that has seen the Londoners fail to score on seven visits and suffer six defeats, including a chastening 3-0 reverse last term that spelt the end for Liam Rosenior.

David Moyes will demand a sharper defensive showing from his side this time around, following a frustrating 2-2 draw with Hull City where a 2-1 lead slipped away. Even so, Everton’s broader defensive record at home offers encouragement, having kept clean sheets in two of their opening three league fixtures at their base.

With both teams eager to build consistency, Saturday’s clash pits Chelsea’s newly found attacking spark against an opponent that traditionally relishes this fixture.

#1401. Comprehensive mapping of essential-gene interactions in M. tuberculosis

Nature (2026) Cite this article

Mycobacterium tuberculosis, the causative agent of tuberculosis, remains the world’s deadliest pathogen1. Despite intensive study, many of its genes remain uncharacterized, which limits the insight that can be gained into tuberculosis biology and constrains drug development. Genetic interaction (GI) mapping is a powerful strategy to define functional relationships between genes by quantifying how the phenotypic effects of combined perturbations deviate from expectations based on single-gene perturbations2,3. Here we develop a dual-sgRNA CRISPR-interference platform that enables high-throughput GI mapping in mycobacteria. We address key technical challenges in library construction and data interpretation by incorporating unique barcodes for each sgRNA pair and implementing a robust statistical pipeline for GI detection. Focusing on essential genes, we generate comprehensive GI maps in the model mycobacterium Mycobacterium smegmatis and the pathogen M. tuberculosis. These maps recapitulate known biology, uncover thousands of previously unrecognized interactions and identify functional connections between essential genes and drug targets. By generating AlphaFold3-based protein–protein interaction predictions4 for all gene pairs in our GI maps, we show that a subset of GIs is likely to reflect underlying physical associations. Validation of selected GIs confirms both novel biological relationships and opportunities for synergistic targeting. Overall, this work establishes a generalizable framework for dual-gene perturbation and defines the architecture of essential-gene networks in mycobacteria, advancing both our understanding of tuberculosis biology and the rational design of combination therapies.

Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb), the world’s leading infectious cause of death1, is among the bacteria that have been most extensively sequenced, but the functions and interactions of many of its genes remain poorly understood. This knowledge gap limits our understanding of the genetic foundations of tuberculosis (TB) and hinders the development of effective therapies.

Genetic interaction (GI) mapping is a powerful approach for deciphering the functional relationships between genes2,3. It involves systematically assessing how perturbing one gene modifies the phenotype associated with perturbing a second gene. A GI is defined as a combined phenotype that deviates from the expectation based on single-gene perturbations. Positive interactions occur when dual perturbation produces a milder phenotype than expected, whereas negative interactions—including synthetic lethal effects—result in a more severe phenotype. Applied at scale, GI mapping yields quantitative interaction profiles that serve as high-resolution phenotypes3. These profiles can generate functional hypotheses for uncharacterized genes, reveal surprising roles for genes of known function and identify connections between distinct biological pathways3. Moreover, they can highlight potential synergistic and antagonistic drug–target relationships, informing combination therapies5.

GI mapping in Mtb has historically been constrained by biological and technical challenges, including slow growth, biosafety requirements and limited early genetic tools. The development of high-density transposon mutagenesis libraries combined with hybridization- or sequencing-based readouts (TnSeq)6,7 constituted a major advance, permitting genome-wide identification of conditionally essential genes8 and GI mapping in deletion mutants9. However, such approaches are typically restricted to non-essential genes, excluding most antibiotic targets. CRISPR interference (CRISPRi) has since emerged as a complementary technique10,11,12,13, enabling conditional and tunable knockdown of both essential and non-essential genes. In bacterial systems, dual-gene knockdowns have been used to identify GIs among small gene sets14, and larger-scale efforts have paired individual deletion or knockdown strains with genome-wide libraries15,16. Dual-CRISPRi and dual-TnSeq approaches for comprehensive GI mapping have been implemented in Bacillus subtilis and Streptococcus pneumoniae17,18,19. However, technical limitations have thus far precluded the development of a comparable system in Mtb.

To enable high-throughput GI mapping in Mtb, we developed a dual-single-guide RNA (sgRNA) CRISPRi platform for mycobacteria. Addressing key challenges in library construction and data analysis, we devised a robust experimental and statistical pipeline for high-confidence detection of GIs. Using this platform, we mapped GIs among nearly all essential genes in Mycobacterium smegmatis (Msm) and Mtb, prioritizing this technically demanding class of genes because of their centrality to cellular processes and importance as antibiotic targets. These maps recapitulate known biological relationships, validating the platform, and also uncover thousands of novel GIs. We further performed AlphaFold3 co-folding for all gene pairs (approximately 600,000) represented in the GI maps, identifying GIs that are likely to reflect physical associations and offering a basis for mechanistic hypotheses. Finally, we validated selected predictions from the maps, including drug–drug interactions and roles in the electron transport chain (ETC) for several genes of unknown function. Together, these maps constitute a powerful resource for elucidating Mtb biology and guiding the rational design of combination therapies.

To enable dual-sgRNA CRISPRi-based GI mapping in Mtb, we adapted the Combinatorial Genetics En Masse (CombiGEM) framework20 to the Mtb CRISPRi platform10, assigning each sgRNA a barcode, and using a cloning workflow that preserves sgRNA–barcode linkage and positions paired barcodes in close proximity (Extended Data Fig. 1a). This design permits accurate quantification of dual-sgRNA strain abundance by barcode sequencing, facilitating high-throughput GI mapping.

GI detection for essential genes requires sgRNAs that impose a precise fitness cost: sufficient to reveal interactions, yet not so severe as to mask additive or synergistic effects. Compounding this challenge, the combinatorial scale of dual-sgRNA libraries necessitates selecting only a small number of sgRNAs per gene. To define the optimal fitness cost for GI detection, we performed a pilot screen in Msm using a panel of 16 genes that are predicted to interact. We selected up to 24 sgRNAs per gene (Supplementary Methods and Supplementary Table 1) spanning a broad range of fitness costs, cloned a dual-sgRNA library containing all pairwise permutations and performed a GI screen using the workflow planned for larger-scale studies (Extended Data Fig. 1b). The resulting data allowed us to identify the sgRNA strength window that best supports GI detection under these conditions: an approximately 8% reduction in fitness per generation (Extended Data Fig. 1c–h and Supplementary Discussion).

To establish feasibility, we built a comprehensive essential-gene GI library in Msm. Guided by the pilot screen, we selected up to two sgRNAs per gene with reproducible, intermediate fitness costs (Fig. 1a and Supplementary Table 1). The library contains 1,524 sgRNAs targeting 787 genes, plus 10 non-targeting (NT) controls, yielding about 2.3 million sgRNA permutations. Target genes included those that are essential for Msm fitness and those that are non-essential in Msm but essential in Mtb; the latter were targeted by the predicted strongest sgRNAs10. The library was cloned in Escherichia coli, validated by deep sequencing (Extended Data Fig. 2a) and transformed into an Msm strain containing a chromosomally encoded Streptococcus thermophilus (Sth1) dCas9 expression cassette. This yielded a pooled library in which each bacterium carries a single integrated guide plasmid expressing two sgRNAs. We subjected this library to competitive growth, tracking dual-sgRNA strain abundance over time by barcode sequencing. Strain depletion was modelled using a piecewise linear regression10, providing a quantitative readout of fitness.

a, Schematic of the screen. (1) Up to two sgRNAs per gene (log2-transformed fold change (L2FC) –1 to –5) were selected. (2) sgRNAs were assigned barcodes (BCs), and all pairwise permutations were generated. (3) The library was passaged with or without anhydrotetracycline (ATc), and L2FC trajectories were computed from barcode counts. (4) GI scores were calculated for each gene pair (see e,f), and genes were clustered by GI profile correlation. (5) Applications of GI data. b, Distribution of observed L2FC at generation 20 for dual non-targeting (NT), single-targeting (A + NT) and dual-targeting (A + B) constructs. c, Correlation of observed L2FC at generation 20 for single-targeting constructs differing only in sgRNA position (Pos1, position 1; Pos2, position 2). d, Multiplicative model of GIs for sgRNAs targeting genes A and B. Fitness outcomes greater or less than expected indicate positive or negative GIs, respectively. e, Example of GI quantification. Left: L2FC trajectories for a representative dnaJ1 + dnaJ2 dual-sgRNA construct. Right: ΔL2FC (observed − expected) trajectories for all eight dnaJ1 + dnaJ2 constructs. f, Expected versus observed L2FC at generation 25 for all dual-targeting constructs. Black line, x = y; red line, generalized additive model (GAM) fit. GI scores were computed as the median GAM residual per gene pair. g, Distribution of GI scores across all gene pairs. Shaded regions denote statistically significant (p > 0.5) interactions. h, Heat map of GI scores for all gene pairs, hierarchically clustered by Pearson correlation of GI profiles. Values beyond ±5 are clipped. i, Number of positive and negative GIs (p > 0.5) per gene. j, Distribution of pairwise GI profile correlations among all sgRNAs, and among sgRNAs targeting the same gene. k, GI scores for all genes paired with murA (left) or with cwlM (right). l, Left, dendrogram of all genes, clustered by GI profile correlation. Branches are coloured by nodes enriched (false discovery rate (FDR) < 0.005) for Gene Ontology (GO) terms by Fisher’s exact test. Right, representative clusters.

Growth phenotypes were highly reproducible across biological replicates (Extended Data Fig. 2b,c). As expected, strains with two NT sgRNAs showed minimal depletion, single-targeting strains exhibited moderate depletion and dual-targeting strains showed the greatest depletion (Fig. 1b). sgRNA position within the plasmid had little effect on fitness, indicating consistent activity from both expression cassettes (Fig. 1c).

To identify GIs, we compared the observed fitness of each dual-targeting strain to the expected outcome under a null model of no interaction (Fig. 1d,e). Deviations from this expectation were quantified and corrected for floor effects (Fig. 1f and Extended Data Fig. 2d,e), and then aggregated at the gene-pair level to generate a GI score. Gene pairs with greater-than-expected depletion were assigned negative GI scores, and those with less-than-expected depletion yielded positive GI scores (Fig. 1d). To assess confidence, GI scores were modelled as a mixture of typical deviations (normal distribution) and deviations outside the norm (uniform distribution). Gene pairs with interaction probabilities of 0.5 < p ≤ 0.95 were designated likely interactions, and those with p > 0.95 confident interactions.

The Msm GI map revealed nearly 8,500 interactions (p > 0.5), with negative GIs outnumbering positive ones (Fig. 1g–i and Supplementary Table 2). This 2.7% hit rate across gene pairs aligns with previous GI studies3. Most genes interacted with fewer than 15 partners, but a subset exhibited high connectivity, consistent with hub-like behaviour that has been observed in other organisms, such as yeast3 (Fig. 1i). Out of 787 targeted genes, 64 (8.1%) showed no interactions under these conditions. Notably, GI strength did not correlate with gene vulnerability10, confirming that our fitness-based sgRNA selection accounts for gene vulnerability (Extended Data Fig. 2f). sgRNAs targeting the same gene exhibited highly correlated interaction profiles (Fig. 1j), underscoring the reproducibility of measured GIs.

Illustrative examples confirm that the map captures known or mechanistically plausible functional relationships. We observed a strong negative GI between the Hsp40 chaperones dnaJ1 and dnaJ2 (Fig. 1e), consistent with their known synthetic lethal relationship21. Another strong negative GI, between cwlM and murA (Fig. 1k), is consistent with the proposed role of CwlM in binding to MurA, stimulating its activity, and promoting peptidoglycan precursor synthesis22.

With individual GIs providing initial confidence in the dataset, we next sought a global assessment of the functional signal encoded in the map. To this end, we analysed correlations among GI profiles, because profile similarity often reflects similar gene function3.

Pairwise correlation and clustering revealed that genes with related biological functions tended to group together (Fig. 1l). We systematically annotated the tree, identifying 63 functionally coherent clusters containing 2 to 48 genes each. Representative clusters spanned functions including cell-wall synthesis, protein degradation, cell division, cofactor and nucleotide synthesis, the ETC, and protein folding and ribosome rescue (Fig. 1l, top to bottom, left to right). Several observations highlight the biological relevance of these clusters. First, cwlM and murA share not only a strong negative GI (Fig. 1k), but also highly correlated GI profiles22 (Fig. 1l). Second, the two genes most closely associated with the mycolic acid transporter mmpL3—pgfA and ttfA—were previously shown to interact physically with MmpL3 and support mycolic acid transport23,24. Third, the transcription factors whiA and whiB2, which are involved in cell division and act in a co-dependent manner in Streptomyces, clustered with each other and with ftsZ, consistent with their established roles25 as transcriptional activators of ftsZ. Many clusters also contained previously uncharacterized genes, as well as functionally annotated genes with unexpected correlations, suggesting unrecognized biological connections. Barring technical limitations (for example, polar effects), these clusters offer functional predictions by placing genes in the context of their network relationships.

Encouraged by the validity of the Msm map, we next extended our approach to Mtb. Following the same experimental blueprint, we constructed a dual-sgRNA library containing up to two sgRNAs per gene with reproducible, intermediate fitness costs (Supplementary Table 1). The library includes 1,483 sgRNAs targeting 762 genes, most of them essential for in vitro Mtb growth, plus 10 NT controls, yielding about 2.2 million sgRNA permutations. The library was cloned in E. coli, validated by deep sequencing (Extended Data Fig. 2a) and transformed into an H37Rv Mtb strain containing a chromosomally integrated Sth1 dCas9 cassette. Competitive growth and barcode sequencing were performed as in Msm.

As in Msm, growth phenotypes were highly reproducible across biological replicates (Extended Data Fig. 2g,h). Dual-NT, single-targeting and dual-targeting strains depleted on average in the expected order, from least to most (Fig. 2a). sgRNA position within the plasmid had a greater effect than it did in Msm (Fig. 2b), but the effect was modest and deemed acceptable, because our GI model accounts for sgRNA position. GIs were quantified, corrected for floor effects (Fig. 2c and Extended Data Fig. 2i,j) and aggregated at the gene-pair level to generate a GI score and confidence estimate, as in Msm.

a, Distribution of observed L2FC at generation 22 for dual-NT, single-targeting and dual-targeting constructs, as in Fig. 1b. b, Correlation of observed L2FC at generation 22 for single-targeting constructs differing only in sgRNA position. c, Expected versus observed L2FC at generation 25 for all dual-targeting constructs. Black line, x = y; red line, GAM fit. GI scores were computed as the median GAM residual per gene pair. d, Distribution of GI scores across all gene pairs. Shaded regions denote statistically significant (p > 0.5) interactions. e, Heat map of GI scores for all gene pairs, hierarchically clustered by Pearson correlation of GI profiles. Values beyond ±5 are clipped. f, Number of positive and negative GIs (p > 0.5) per gene. g, Distribution of pairwise GI profile correlations among all sgRNAs, and among sgRNAs targeting the same gene. h, GI scores for all genes paired with dnaJ1 (left) or with dnaJ2 (right). i, GI scores for all genes paired with murA (left) or with cwlM (right). j, GI scores for all genes paired with secA1 (left) or with secF (right). k, Left, dendrogram of all genes, clustered by GI profile correlation. Branches are coloured by nodes enriched (FDR < 0.005) for GO terms by Fisher’s exact test. Right, representative clusters (from top to bottom: fatty acid biosynthesis, arginine biosynthesis, nucleotide biosynthesis, folate metabolism, thiamine metabolism, menaquinone biosynthesis and protein degradation).

The Mtb GI map revealed nearly 6,500 interactions (p > 0.5), with negative GIs outnumbering positive ones (Fig. 2d–f and Supplementary Table 3). This 2.2% hit rate across all gene pairs parallels the Msm map. Most genes interacted with fewer than 12 partners, but a subset exhibited high connectivity (Fig. 2f), and 3.4% (26/762) of targeted genes showed no interactions under these conditions. As in Msm, sgRNAs targeting the same gene exhibited highly correlated interaction profiles (Fig. 2g), and GI strength did not correlate with gene vulnerability (Extended Data Fig. 2k). We observed strong negative GIs between dnaJ1 and dnaJ2 (ref. 21) and between cwlM and murA (ref. 22) (Fig. 2h,i). Further strong negative GIs recapitulated known or mechanistically plausible functional relationships, including (1) transcription factors and their targets (Extended Data Fig. 3a–c); (2) partially redundant enzymes (Extended Data Fig. 3d,e); and (3) functionally related genes within shared biological processes (Fig. 2j and Extended Data Fig. 3f). Reflecting the biological coherence of the data, clustering by GI profile similarity grouped genes with related functions (Fig. 2k).

To test platform reproducibility, we repeated the Mtb GI screen using a slightly higher concentration of anhydrotetracycline (ATc) to ensure saturating induction of dCas9 and sgRNA (Supplementary Table 3). We refer to the original and replicate screens as experiment 1 and experiment 2, respectively. The second screen showed slightly greater positional variability but also more pronounced depletion of single- and dual-targeting constructs (Extended Data Fig. 4a,b), resulting in a wider distribution of GI scores (Extended Data Fig. 4c–e) and a higher signal-to-noise ratio. Key benchmarks were again met, including concordance among replicates (Extended Data Fig. 2l–o), high GI profile similarity among sgRNAs targeting the same gene (Extended Data Fig. 4f) and a lack of correlation between GI score and gene vulnerability (Extended Data Fig. 2p). Most importantly, the replicate map recapitulated the functional information in the original. Summary metrics, including the overall hit rate (2.3%) and per-gene interaction number (Extended Data Fig. 4g), were comparable; specific GIs were reproduced across the two screens (Extended Data Figs. 3g–l and 4h,i); and functionally related genes clustered together (Extended Data Fig. 4j).

GI scores were strongly correlated between the Mtb experiments (R = 0.82; Extended Data Fig. 4k). However, concordance between interaction probabilities was lower (Supplementary Table 3), particularly near the boundary between the null and interaction distributions, where experiment-specific fits diverged. To reconcile these differences, we extended our statistical framework to jointly model GI scores from both experiments (Extended Data Fig. 4k). The model assigns each gene pair a joint probability and, when sufficiently confident, classifies the interaction as negative, positive or discordant. Joint modelling identified confident GIs for approximately 2.5% of Mtb gene pairs (p > 0.95) and likely GIs for 4.4% (p > 0.5).

Given the substantial but incomplete overlap between the two maps, we retained data from both screens. Unless otherwise specified, the individual Mtb GI scores and downstream analyses presented in the following sections are based on experiment 2, and the joint model provides an integrated assessment of interaction confidence across both experiments.

Having established platform robustness in both Mtb and Msm, we analysed GIs involving homologous genes targeted in both libraries. Consistent with comparative GI work in budding and fission yeast26, homologues showed a modestly higher GI profile correlation than did non-homologues (Fig. 3a,b), reflecting a mixture of conserved (for example, Figs. 1e,k and 2h,i) and non-conserved (for example, Extended Data Fig. 5a–c) interactions. A global comparison of GI scores for homologous gene pairs revealed limited correlation across species (R = 0.26; Extended Data Fig. 5d), which increased substantially when the analysis was restricted to gene pairs sharing the same biological process annotation (R = 0.57; Extended Data Fig. 5e and Supplementary Table 4). Likewise, within-process GIs were conserved at a higher rate than the overall set of interactions (Extended Data Fig. 5f). Together, these findings indicate that mycobacteria recapitulate the pattern of GI conservation observed in budding and fission yeast, in which interactions that link genes in the same biological process are preferentially conserved relative to interactions that link distinct processes26.

We next examined the functional organization of Mtb GIs by testing for enrichment of interactions within and between biological processes (Supplementary Table 4). We focused on negative GIs, because they are more abundant in our dataset and more likely to reflect functional relationships, following the precedent in yeast3. Gene pairs comprising genes in the same biological process were enriched for negative GIs (on-diagonal; Fig. 3c and Extended Data Fig. 5g), consistent with limited tolerance for simultaneous knockdown within essential pathways. Negative GIs were also enriched among gene pairs spanning distinct biological processes—for example, genes involved in synthesizing different components of the cell envelope (such as arabinogalactan and lipoarabinomannan), and genes involved in DNA replication and DNA repair (off-diagonal; Fig. 3c and Extended Data Fig. 5g). Beyond these process-level patterns, gene pairs with highly correlated GI profiles were themselves enriched for negative GIs (Extended Data Fig. 4l), consistent with the expectation that genes acting in the same pathway are more likely to share interaction partners and interact with each other3.

To investigate the molecular basis of GIs, we asked how frequently they reflect physical associations. Because no large-scale experimental protein–protein interaction (PPI) map exists for Mtb, we generated PPI predictions using pooled AlphaFold3 co-folding4,27 across the approximately 600,000 gene pairs screened in the Mtb and Msm GI libraries. We identified 15,240 candidate PPIs using a size-corrected interface predicted template modelling score (s.c. ipTM) cut-off ≥ 0.05 (Fig. 3d,e, Extended Data Fig. 6a–h and Supplementary Tables 2 and 3). Because size correction systematically reduces ipTM scores, this threshold is necessarily permissive, yet the overall hit rate (2.6%) remains low. Many of these candidates achieve higher ipTM scores when evaluated pairwise with AlphaFold-Multimer28. Consistent with observations in yeast3, gene pairs with negative GIs or highly correlated GI profiles were enriched for predicted physical interactions (Fig. 3f). Nevertheless, many lacked a predicted PPI, because GIs can arise from pathway-, process- or network-level relationships without direct binding. Overall, this resource identifies gene pairs that are both genetically and physically linked, providing a framework for predicting their molecular mechanisms. We present several representative examples spanning both known22,29,30,31 (Fig. 3g–j) and previously unrecognized (Fig. 3k–n) biological connections.

Previous studies have shown that GIs can predict drug–drug interactions5. To test whether this principle holds in our dataset, we analysed GIs among established drug targets.

One of the strongest negative GIs in both Mtb and Msm involved aspC (alanine aminotransferase16,32) and ddl (d-alanine-d-alanine ligase; Fig. 4a). Although previously unknown, this interaction is mechanistically plausible: AspC is crucial for biosynthesis of l-Ala, which is required by Alr (alanine racemase) to produce d-Ala, the substrate for Ddl (Fig. 4b). aspC also showed a negative GI with alr. Alr and Ddl are the targets of d-cycloserine33, a second-line agent for multidrug-resistant TB. Consistent with the GI data, CRISPRi-based chemical–genetic interaction (CGI) profiling of d-cycloserine identified aspC as one of the top sensitizing hits (Fig. 4c,d and Supplementary Table 5). Moreover, a paper published while we revised this one reported synergy between an AspC inhibitor and d-cycloserine34.

Another set of novel, mechanistically plausible interactions involved PptT, a phosphopantetheinyl transferase that activates acyl carrier proteins (ACPs) required for lipid biosynthesis and is an active drug development target35. PptT showed negative GIs with kasA, hadB and hadC (Fig. 4e), which catalyse steps in the FAS-II pathway responsible for mycolic acid biosynthesis (Fig. 4f), and are likewise being pursued as drug targets36,37. Consistent with the GI data, CGI profiling of thiolactomycin, a KasA and KasB inhibitor, identified pptT as a top sensitizing hit (Extended Data Fig. 7a and Supplementary Table 5). Moreover, co-treating Mtb with thiolactomycin and the PptT inhibitor 8918 produced strong synergy in both the H37Rv reference and clinical Mtb strains38 representing diverse lineages (Fig. 4g,h). This synergy was specific: neither thiolactomycin nor 8918 synergized with control drug treatments (Extended Data Fig. 7b–g). Although KasA inhibitors and rifampicin are synergistic39, kasA and rifampicin’s target rpoB did not show a negative GI (Supplementary Table 3). In this case, KasA inhibition is likely to potentiate rifampicin by increasing envelope permeability and intracellular rifampicin exposure, rather than through a target-based mechanism39. Supporting this interpretation, knockdown of rpoB did not sensitize to thiolactomycin in our CGI screen (Extended Data Fig. 7a). These examples show how KasA inhibition can drive synergy through both target-specific and chemotype-specific mechanisms, and how GI mapping can disentangle these modes of action. Combined inhibition of PptT and the HadAB and HadBC dehydratases likewise produced strong synergy (Fig. 4i,j), providing further evidence that negative GIs can predict drug–drug interactions.

To assess whether positive GIs likewise have predictive value, we focused on the pks13–efpA pair. Pks13 and EfpA are essential proteins involved in mycolic acid biosynthesis and lipid translocation, respectively, and both are active targets for TB drug development40,41. The pair showed a strong positive GI (Fig. 4k), predicting drug–drug antagonism, which was confirmed by checkerboard assays of preclinical Pks13 and EfpA inhibitors (Fig. 4l and Extended Data Fig. 7h,i).

As a final proof-of-concept, we examined PknA and PknB, essential eukaryotic-like serine/threonine kinases that regulate Mtb growth and division and are promising drug targets42. pknA and pknB exhibited strong negative GIs with embA and embB (Fig. 4m), which encode arabinogalactan biosynthetic enzymes targeted by the first-line TB drug ethambutol43. Co-treatment with ethambutol and the PknA and PknB inhibitor V49 resulted in borderline synergy in checkerboard assays (Extended Data Fig. 7j), but clear synergy in bacterial killing assays (Fig. 4n). This bactericidal interaction seemed to be specific: pknA and pknB did not exhibit negative GIs with ATP synthase genes (Fig. 4m), and V49 did not enhance killing by the ATP synthase inhibitor bedaquiline44 (Fig. 4n). Although V49 and bedaquiline showed borderline synergy in checkerboard assays (Extended Data Fig. 7k), this might reflect the same uptake-mediated effect proposed for KasA inhibition and rifampicin, rather than a target-based interaction39. Together, these results illustrate how GI mapping can reveal combination effects that are missed by conventional growth-inhibition assays.

Beyond the specific interactions discussed above, the Mtb GI map offers broader opportunities for drug discovery. Strong GIs between currently pursued TB drug targets are rare, consistent with the general scarcity of target-based synergy and antagonism45. Nonetheless, the map reveals thousands of previously unexplored interactions among established and potential drug targets across diverse pathways. We cover several of these interactions in the Supplementary Discussion and Extended Data Figs. 8 and 9. The map also identifies a set of ‘pleiotropic sensitizers’—including ppk, macE, dnaA, rnc, treS, sodA and pknG—that showed strong negative GIs across numerous targets, consistent with findings from our previous CGI studies39. Inhibitors of these pleiotropic sensitizers could potentiate multiple drug classes by globally altering bacterial metabolism, stress responses or regulatory networks, making these genes promising candidates for combination therapy aimed at amplifying the activity of diverse antibacterial agents.

Oxidative phosphorylation—the combined activities of the ETC and ATP synthase—has emerged as an important antibiotic target in Mtb and related pathogens. Clinically validated examples include the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA)-approved ATP synthase inhibitor bedaquiline44 and telacebec (Q203)46, a clinical drug candidate that targets complex III. In mycobacteria, complex III2IV2 (Fig. 5a) is the primary terminal oxidase that establishes the proton gradient driving ATP synthesis47. This supercomplex (larger than 700 kDa) consists of 24 protein subunits47 that position 18 redox cofactors to enable electron transfer coupled with proton translocation. In eukaryotes, numerous proteins chaperoning the maturation of complex III and IV have been identified, and defects in these assembly factors cause severe hereditary diseases48. In mycobacteria, the mechanisms of complex III2IV2 assembly and cofactor incorporation remain mostly unknown49.

We identified a cluster of genes of unknown function that strongly correlated with genes encoding subunits of complex III2IV2 and with genes involved in cofactor biogenesis, in both Msm and Mtb (Figs. 1l and 5b,c and Extended Data Fig. 10a). Many of these uncharacterized genes also showed negative GIs with the alternative, partially redundant terminal oxidase, cytochrome bd oxidase (cyt. bd), encoded by cydA and cydB (Fig. 5d,e). Synthetic lethality with cyt. bd is a hallmark of defects in complex III2IV2 in mycobacteria50. We thus hypothesized that these genes contribute to the assembly or function of complex III2IV2. Several lines of evidence support this hypothesis: (1) independent single-strain knockdowns using sgRNAs not included in the screen validated the GI results in both Msm and Mtb (Fig. 5f–i); (2) complementation experiments in Msm ruled out off-target effects and established the functional equivalence of Mtb homologues (Extended Data Fig. 10b); (3) these genes showed negative GIs with each other in Mtb (Extended Data Fig. 10c); (4) AlphaFold3 predictions suggest physical interactions among several of these genes and with CtaD, a complex IV subunit (Fig. 5j,k and Extended Data Fig. 10d); and (5) knockdown of these genes in strains lacking cyt. bd reduced oxygen consumption, an indicator of complex III2IV2 activity (Fig. 5l and Extended Data Fig. 10e–g), and increased sensitivity to Q203 to varying extents (Fig. 5m and Extended Data Fig. 10h).

To extend these findings biochemically, we focused on ms2764, selected for its AlphaFold3-predicted interactions and the tractability of generating a functional 3×Flag-tagged construct with correct membrane topology. To our knowledge, there are no previous studies of ms2764 or its Mtb homologue rv2698, which encode membrane proteins containing a DUF3093 domain that seems to be restricted to Actinobacteria. Affinity purification of Ms2764–3×Flag followed by mass spectrometry (AP–MS) showed co-purification of complex III2IV2 subunits and several other uncharacterized genes in the cluster (Fig. 5n). Motivated by this evidence of physical interaction, we generated an ms2764 knockout and assayed respiratory activity in inverted membrane vesicles (IMVs). As shown previously51, NADH-driven IMV acidification can occur even when complex III2IV2 is inhibited or absent, whereas succinate-driven IMV acidification requires functional complex III2IV2. Similar to IMVs from a ∆qcrB strain, ∆ms2764 IMVs were capable of NADH-driven acidification but not succinate-driven acidification, indicating loss of complex III2IV2 activity (Fig. 5o) and providing biochemical evidence that Ms2764 contributes to complex function.

Closer inspection of these uncharacterized genes revealed that one (rv2235 or ms4311; here renamed surf1) contains a well-conserved SURF1 domain, known in other species to facilitate the incorporation of haem a3 into CtaD (ref. 49). A second gene (rv0102 or ms4702; here renamed ctiP) probably encodes a distant CtiP homologue (25% sequence identity) that, in Corynebacterium, seems to mediate CuB insertion into CtaD (ref. 49). Consistent with this proposed role, ctiP is encoded adjacent to chalkophore biosynthesis genes in Mtb, which supply copper to complex IV under copper-limiting conditions and during infection52. This genomic context suggests that CtiP collaborates with chalkophores to metallate complex IV. rv1342c (ms4900) and lprD are induced under iron starvation53, consistent with the iron dependence of complex III2IV2 activity, whereas rv1457c (ms3118) and rv1458c (ms3119) are located immediately upstream of ctaA, which catalyses the final step of haem A biosynthesis. For the remaining genes, no precedent links them to the ETC. They encode predicted integral membrane proteins (rv2698 (ms2764) and rv1083 (ms5260)) and lipoproteins (lppL, rv2980 (ms2396)). These uncharacterized genes might therefore participate in cofactor trafficking or installation or represent previously unrecognized subunits of complex III2IV2. Although further studies are required to define their molecular roles, these findings show how our GI platform enables hypothesis generation for previously uncharacterized genes.

A large portion of the Mtb genome remains poorly understood. Here, to help close this gap, we developed a scalable approach for mapping genetic interactions in mycobacteria, focusing on essential genes because they underpin core cellular processes and represent the targets of most antibiotics. Across the model species Msm and the pathogen Mtb, we screened more than four million sgRNA permutations and identified more than 15,000 GIs. This constitutes the first comprehensive GI map of essential genes in Mtb—and, to our knowledge, the first such map for essential genes in any organism beyond budding yeast3. Together with other large-scale resources41,54,55,56,57—including transcriptomic and metabolomic compendia, systematic gene knockdown and morphological profiling, curated TnSeq datasets and chemical–genetic profiling—these datasets unlock new opportunities for dissecting mycobacterial biology and guiding the rational design of drug combinations.

Three applications of our maps merit particular attention. First, they can identify interactions between drug targets, enabling prediction of synergistic or antagonistic drug combinations. Second, GI profile similarity can reveal functionally related genes. Third, GI mapping can uncover surprising links between well-characterized genes and distinct biological processes. Although some unexpected associations might reflect technical artefacts (for example, off-target or polar effects), many are likely to reveal genuine biology. For example, the ribonuclease III gene rnc, best known for rRNA maturation58 and CRISPR RNA processing59, clusters with cell-division genes in both Mtb and Msm (Fig. 1l). This association aligns with observations60 in Corynebacterium glutamicum, in which Rnc cleaves the mRNA of the cell-division regulator MraZ.

Shortening the duration of TB treatment remains a central objective in TB drug development. One promising strategy is to exploit interactions between drug targets. GI mapping, already a powerful approach in cancer therapeutics3, offers analogous opportunities for TB. First, GI maps can highlight synergistic and antagonistic target combinations to exploit and to avoid, guiding the rational selection of drug combinations. We validated four synergistic compound pairs (8918 + TLM, 8918 + TAZ, 8918 + ISO and V49 + EMB) and one antagonistic pair (BRD-8000.3 + mCMX410) predicted by our GI maps. We also identified and validated numerous negative GIs that link established drug targets to genes not currently targeted pharmacologically. These findings nominate the corresponding gene products as potential targets for future drug development. GI data can also illuminate the mechanistic basis of drug–drug synergy—distinguishing, for example, uptake-based and target-specific interactions. Moreover, because pairwise interactions might predict higher-order interactions61, these datasets provide a foundation for exploring regimen-level effects. This information represents a key piece of the puzzle, although other factors beyond drug synergies contribute to therapeutic success62. Second, GI maps can help to ‘de-orphan’ potential drug targets by predicting their function—an essential step, because understanding a target’s biochemical role is a prerequisite for target-based drug discovery. Third, GI profiles provide genetic signatures for inferring the mechanisms of action of uncharacterized compounds. A close resemblance between a compound’s CGI profile and a gene’s GI profile could implicate that gene as the compound’s primary target5. Two caveats are worth noting.
