a) Projections of the distribution of every fly over the first 15 min of representative 40-min group assays with 5 males and 5 females in a large 190 mm arena with a 21.5 mm central food patch (red circle) formed from agar perfumed with ACV (orange) or an agar control (blue) for D. erecta (left) and D. melanogaster (right). The positions of each fly in every 250th frame are overlaid, projecting a total of 108 frames over 15 min. b) Population occupancy of the central patch over time for 40-min group assays with 5 males and 5 females in a large 190 mm arena with a 21.5 mm central food patch for D. erecta (above) and D. melanogaster (below). Occupancy ranges from 0 with no individuals on the patch to 1 when all 10 individuals of the group are located on the central patch at a given time. Means ± standard error are indicated in black and shaded regions for assays on an ACV (orange) or agar patch (blue). Patch occupancies of individual assays are shown in shaded lines (n = 10 each). c) Fraction of individuals of group assays in (b) within 3 fly body lengths of one other fly (paired, black), in a group of three or more flies (grouped, dark grey), or at a distance over 3 body lengths from any other individual (solo, light grey) over time for D. erecta (above) and D. melanogaster (below). All flies in the entire arena were included in the analysis. Means ± standard errors are indicated. d) Total amount of time at least one group of three or more flies is present in assays with 5 males and 5 females in a large 190 mm arena with a 21.5 mm central food patch formed from agar perfumed with ACV (orange) or an agar control (blue) for D. erecta (D. ere) and D. melanogaster (D. mel). Means (black bars) and individual assays (dots, n = 10 each) are shown. e) Mean number of flies in large arena (190 mm) group assays (5 males and 5 females) present in clusters of three or more individuals throughout the whole 40-min assay for D. erecta (D. ere) and D. melanogaster (D. mel) in the presence of an agar (blue) or ACV (orange) patch. Assay means (dots, n = 10 each) and overall mean (black bar) are shown. f) and g) Mean distance of individuals in large 190 mm arena from the central 21.5 mm food patch formed from agar and perfumed with ACV (orange) or an agar control (blue) (f) and number of patch visits (g) for D. erecta (D. ere, agar n = 70 flies from 7 assays; ACV n = 100 flies from 10 assays) and D. melanogaster (D. mel; n = 100 flies from 10 assays, each) over 40 min. Black bars indicate the mean. h) Fraction of all copulations per large 190 mm arena group assay (5 males and 5 females; n = 10 assays each) that commenced on the central 21.5 mm patch formed from agar perfumed with ACV (orange) or an agar control (blue) for D. erecta (D. ere) and D. melanogaster (D. mel). i) Raster plots depicting the position of each individual fly relative to the Pandanus patch over duration of the assay (n = 6 assays) for D. erecta (left) and D. melanogaster (right). Time on the patch is highlighted in yellow. Greyscale indicates linear distance to the patch with decreasing distance shaded in lighter shades of grey. Individuals are aligned by the time of their first entry to the patch. j) Comparison of the spatial distribution of copulations in the presence of a Pandanus patch (yellow dots) for D. erecta (left) and D. melanogaster (right) (n = 6 assays). k) Mean patch occupancy for all flies for D. erecta (D. ere) and D. melanogaster (D. mel) (n = 6 assays). l) Fraction of all copulations that were initiated on the central food patch for D. erecta (D. ere) and D. melanogaster (D. mel). Each dot represents a separate assay (n = 6) and bars represent the mean. Scale bar indicates relative density. All statistical tests performed were two-sided, where appropriate. Comparisons that were statistically significant are indicated as: *p ≤ 0.05; **p < 0.001; ***p < 0.0001; all other tests were not statistically significant. See Supplementary Table 1 for full statistics.

a) Mean relative distribution of flies in small 38 mm arena group assays with 5 males and 5 females in the presence of a central 21.5 mm food patch (red circle) formed from agar perfumed with ACV (right) or an agar control (left) for D. erecta (above; agar n = 8, ACV n = 7) and D. melanogaster (below; agar n = 6, ACV n = 6). b) Interaction per minute of all five D. erecta males of 5 male and 5 female group assays in small 38 mm arenas with a central 21.5 mm food patch towards any other individual in the arena for D. erecta (D. ere; agar n = 8, ACV n = 7) and D. melanogaster (D. mel; agar n = 6, ACV n = 6). Individual males (dots) and means (black bars) are indicated for assays with ACV (orange) or an agar (blue) patch. c) Interactions of all five males towards any other individual in the arena over the duration of an assay (top, solid line represents mean and shaded line individual assays) and ethogram of each male for either agar (blue; n = 8) or ACV (orange; n = 7) showing individual interactions with other males (open circle) and females (closed circle). Top panels and assays 5,8,11 and 15 are replotted from Fig. 1m. d) Approaches per minute of individual males towards a single female, another male, or an inanimate fly-sized hemispherical visual target (⌀ ca. 3 mm) in a small 38 mm arena with a central ACV (orange) or agar (blue) patch for D. erecta (top; targets: female: agar n = 16, ACV n = 19, male: agar n = 17, ACV n = 20, bead: agar n = 18, ACV n = 15) and D. melanogaster (bottom; targets: female: n = 8, each, male: agar n = 24, ACV n = 26, bead: n = 8, each). Means (black bar) for all assays (dots) are indicated. All males were paired with a single mobile target (another male or female), or a single hemispherical bead positioned at the center of the arena. e) Courtship index of flies in small 38 mm arena group assays with 5 males and 5 females in the presence of a central 21.5 mm food patch (red circle) formed from agar perfumed with ACV (right) or an agar control (left) for different D. melanogaster lines derived from populations in North America (Canton-S (CS); n = 6 assays) and Africa (Cameroon (CO4n); n = 4 assays and Rwanda (RG11n); agar n = 5, ACV n = 6 assays). CS data are replotted from Fig. 1h. All statistical tests performed were two-sided, where appropriate. Those comparisons that were statistically significant are indicated as: *p ≤ 0.05; ***p < 0.0001; all other tests were not statistically significant. See Supplementary Table 1 for full statistics. Schematics in d adapted from ref. 43, Springer Nature Limited.

a) Schematic depicting assay in which a single male was provided a female-sized hemispherical bead (ca. 3 mm) at the center of a small 38 mm arena with a 21.5 mm central food patch (red circle) formed from agar perfumed with ACV or an agar control. b) Fraction of time individual D. erecta (D. ere, left, agar n = 18, ACV n = 15) and D. melanogaster (D. mel, right, n = 8) males (dots) spent within three body-lengths of the hemispherical bead at the center of a small arena in the presence of an ACV (orange) or agar (blue) patch over 20 min. Mean is indicated by black bars. c) Mean velocity of flies in b). d) Frequency distribution of the central hemispherical bead position relative to the heading direction of D. erecta (top, n = 15–18) and D. melanogaster (bottom, n = 8) males in (b) on an agar (blue, left) or an ACV (orange, right) patch. Coordinates are shown using orientations of all males over 20 min with respect to the egocentric orientation of the male, heading towards the bead at 0/2π, while the bead is behind the male at π. e) Schematic of a fly head highlighting olfactory appendages (third antennal segments and maxillary palps) innervated by Orco+ olfactory sensory neurons in green and innervation of antennal lobes in the brain (center). Right: Schematic of optogenetics bead assay comprised of a single male with a female-sized hemispherical bead (⌀ ca. 3 mm) at the center in a small 38 mm arena with a 21.5 mm central agar patch. Arena is fitted with LEDs emitting 625 nm (red) light from top. f) Left: Overlaid trajectories of D. erecta (top, n = 13) and D. melanogaster (bottom, n = 12) Orco>CsChrimson control males reared without retinal over the 2 min prior to (left, pre) and during 2-min (right, LED on) optogenetic activation. Right: Raster of individual bead approaches (circles) for each male in the 2 min prior to and during optogenetic activation (grey shaded area). g) Mean distribution of males in 38 mm arenas with one isolated male in the presence of a central 21.5 mm food patch (red circle) formed from agar perfumed with ACV (right) or an agar control (left) for D. erecta (n = 4). No visual target was provided in these assays. Scale bar indicates relative density. h) Top left: Schematic of grid assay containing a lattice of 13 fly-sized hemispherical visual targets (⌀ ca. 3 mm) arranged in a regular square array in a large 190 mm arena on a large 145 mm food patch (red circle) formed from agar perfumed with ACV or an agar control. Bead sizes are enlarged and not to scale to highlight grid pattern. Top right: Mean distribution of groups of 5 D. erecta males on ACV without lattice of hemispherical visual targets over 20 min (n = 5 assays). Bottom: Mean distribution of groups of 5 D. erecta males in the presence of lattice on an agar (left) or ACV (right) patch (n = 5 assays, each). Scale bar indicates relative density over 20 min. i) Number of times any single D. erecta male within the group of 5 males switched from one hemispherical visual bead target to another on an agar (blue, left) or an ACV (orange, right) patch (n = 5 assays, 5 males each) over 20 min. j) Top: Overlaid trajectories of individual D. erecta males on agar (left) and ACV (right) in the presence of the bead grid (n = 8 assays) over 20 min. Bottom: Mean distribution of individual D. erecta males on an agar (left) or ACV (right) patch in the presence of a bead lattice. Scale bar indicates relative density. k) Overlaid trajectories of groups of 5 D. melanogaster males on agar (left) and ACV (right) in the presence of the bead grid (n = 5 assays) over 20 min. l) Mean number of approaches per male in (k) for each bead in the grid over 20 min indicated by color and size of the circle. m) Four representative assays from (k) for agar (left) and ACV (right), in which bead approaches for each male (rows) are depicted (black dots) over the 20-min assay. n) and o) Total number of beads in the grid visited (n) and approaches per minute (o) for each individual male in (k) on agar (blue, n = 25 males) and ACV (orange, n = 25 males). p) The number of song bouts per bead approached for D. erecta males in grid assay containing a lattice of 13 fly-sized hemispherical visual targets in a large 190 mm arena on a large 145 mm food patch formed from agar perfumed with ACV (orange, n = 8) or an agar control (blue, n = 8). Individual males were alone in the assay chamber and behavior was scored for all approaches during 20-min assay. q) Distance of a male to the immobilized decapitated female (black) and the closest bead in representative grid assay shown in Fig. 2m with the bead in the second row on the left replaced by an immobilized decapitated female over 20 min. Red dotted line indicates one fly length (3 mm) distance. Once male has encountered the female, he remains close to her for the remainder of the assay, moving farther from the rest of the beads. r) Average fraction of time a male spent with each bead prior to encountering the female (black dots) and fraction of time male spent with the female after encountering her (green dots) for all males that encountered the female on ACV (n = 8). All statistical tests performed were two-sided, where appropriate. Those comparisons that were statistically significant are indicated as: n.s.: not significant; *p < 0.05; **p < 0.001; ***p < 0.0001. See Supplementary Table 1 for full statistics. Schematics in e adapted from ref. 43, Springer Nature Limited.

a) Schematic showing virtual reality behavioral setup for tethered flies provided with an oscillating visual target (black dot) and with ACV presented through odor tube. b) Target position in the male visual field (top) and corresponding heading direction (center) and tracking index (bottom) of a representative D. erecta male prior to (black), during (orange), and after (black) presentation of ACV with visual target continuously oscillating after an initial 30 s baseline period. c) Tracking indices (TI) of eight wild type D. erecta males prior to (black), during (orange), and after (black) presentation of ACV with continuously oscillating visual target (black arrow) as in (b). d) Left: Mean tracking index of wild type D. erecta males (n = 8, same males shown in c), prior to (black), during (orange), and after (black) presentation of ACV with continuously oscillating visual target (black arrow). Thick lines represent the mean, shaded areas the standard error. Right: Probability of tracking. e) Same as in d) but with D. erecta males mutant for the chemosensory co-receptors Orco and Ir8a (n = 4) deficient in the major olfactory pathways previously implicated in the detection of ACV volatiles60,61. f) Left: Tracking index of D. erecta males expressing CsChrimson in Orco+ olfactory sensory neurons in the antenna and maxillary palps prior to (pre), during (LED) and after (post) optogenetic activation (n = 3). Lines indicate mean ± standard error (shaded). Right: Probability of tracking. All statistical tests performed were two-sided, where appropriate. Those comparisons that were statistically significant are indicated as: *p ≤ 0.05; all other tests were not statistically significant. See Supplementary Table 1 for full statistics. Schematic in a adapted from ref. 38, Springer Nature Limited.

a) and b) P1 neural activity (∆F/F) of D. erecta (a) and D. melanogaster (b) males plotted against tracking index for five individuals (rows) for the entire experiment (all), during the 30 s baseline period (baseline), and with a continuously oscillating visual target prior to (vis, pre), during presentation of visual stimulus and ACV (vis + acv) and after (vis, post) presentation of ACV with only visual target. Line of best fit (red), Pearson correlation coefficient and p-value are indicated for each plot. See Supplementary Table 1 for full statistics.

a) Schematic of LC10a neurons and region of interest imaged (black box). b) LC10a neural activity (∆F/F) recorded in the right hemisphere of a representative D. erecta (left) and D. melanogaster (right) male tracking an oscillating visual target plotted against the position of the target (black line) in the male visual field colored by the target’s progressive (black) and regressive (grey) movement. ACV was provided throughout. c) Target position in the male visual field (top), corresponding LC10a neural activity (center), and heading direction (bottom) for a representative D. erecta male in the presence of ACV during an initial 10 s baseline period and then with visual target continuously oscillating. d) Schematic of fru+ innervation of the Lateral Protocerebral Complex (LPC, green) and Anterior Optic Tubercle (AOTu, red) and ROI used to image both neuropils simultaneously (black box). e) and h) Left: Neural activity (∆F/F) of aggregate Fruitless (Fru+) neurons in the lateral protocerebral complex (LPC) innervated by P1 neurons. Top: Neural activity. Arrow indicates appearance of visual target. Neural activity in LPC and AOTu was imaged simultaneously for each male. Right: Mean neural activity (top, bottom) and probability to track (center) before, during, and after presentation of ACV. f) and i) Left: Neural activity (∆F/F) of aggregate Fruitless (Fru+) neurons in the anterior optic tubercle (AOTu) innervated by LC10a axons. Top: Neural activity. Center: tracking index of males prior to (black), during (orange), and after (black) presentation of ACV with visual target continuously oscillating after an initial 30 s baseline period. a) Courtship index of D. erecta males paired with a D. melanogaster female in small 38 mm arenas with a central 21.5 mm food patch formed from agar perfumed with ACV. Males were either wild type (black, n = 8) or mutant for the DEG/ENaC sodium channel ppk23 (red, n = 7). Courtship indices for the entire 40 min of the assay (left) or the 10 min following courtship initiation are shown. Black lines indicate mean. Enhanced courtship in mutants is consistent with evidence from other species that ppk23 is essential to detection of heterospecific pheromones, suggesting that D. erecta remain averse to courting D. melanogaster females on ACV due to detection of heterospecific pheromones by ppk23+ sensory neurons. Black line indicates mean. b) Mean velocity of individual female and male D. erecta (left) and D. melanogaster (right) in pairs (1m1f, Dere n = 20, each, Dmel n = 8, each) or groups of 5 males and 5 females (5m5f, Dere agar n = 8, ACV n = 7 assays, Dmel n = 6, each) in small 38 mm arenas with a central 21.5 mm food patch formed from agar perfumed with ACV (orange) or an agar control (blue). Individual (dots) and overall means (black line) are indicated. c) Fraction of time male (left) and female (right) D. erecta (D. ere) and D. melanogaster (D. mel) in b) spent moving when paired (1m1f) or in groups (5m5f) over 40 min in a small 38 mm arena with a central 21.5 mm food patch on agar (blue) or ACV (orange). Black lines indicate mean. d) Mean velocity of individual D. erecta (left) and D. melanogaster (right) males in small 38 mm arenas with a central 21.5 mm food patch formed from agar perfumed with ACV (orange) or an agar control (blue). Individual (dots) and overall means (black line) are indicated (n = 10, each). e) Mean velocity of all other males and females in the group during the 2 s window preceding a male courtship bout, compared to a permuted null distribution of 2-s velocity windows in D. erecta groups on agar (left, n = 8 assays) and ACV (right, n = 7 assays). f) Movement probability of a female target for D. erecta (left) and D. melanogaster (right) 1 male and 1 female pair assays in small 38 mm arenas with a central 21.5 mm food patch for the whole 40-min assay (filled circle) and the five second period before the male engages in courtship (open circle) on agar (blue, Dere n = 20, Dmel n = 8) or ACV (orange, Dere n = 20, Dmel n = 8). All statistical tests performed were two-sided, where appropriate. Those comparisons that were statistically significant are indicated as: *p ≤ 0.05; ***p < 0.0001; all other tests were not statistically significant. See Supplementary Table 1 for full statistics.

Male brains stained for GFP (green) and neuropil counterstain (magenta) visualizing neural expression patterns of transgenic lines labeling olfactory sensory neurons a) and b) (Orco-Gal4), LC10a neurons c) and d) (VT029314-Gal4), and sexually dimorphic neurons expressing the fruitless e) and f) (Fru-Gal4) and g) and h) (Dsx-Gal4) transcription factors. Scalebars: 50 µm.

Group behaviour in a large arena with central food patch. Representative video clips of D. erecta and D. melanogaster groups of five males and five females in large 190-mm arenas with a central food patch filled with agar perfumed with ACV (orange) or an agar-only control (blue). Clips displayed at 30× speed.

Groups in small arena with central food patch. Representative clips of D. erecta and D. melanogaster groups of five males and five females in small 38-mm arenas with a central food patch filled with agar perfumed with ACV (orange) or an agar-only control (blue). Clips displayed at 10× speed.

Behaviour of individual males towards an inanimate bead. Video comparing behaviour of individual D. erecta and D. melanogaster males in a small 38-mm arena towards a central hemispherical plastic bead of 3 mm diameter on ACV (orange) or an agar control (blue). Recordings are displayed at 10× speed.

Optogenetic activation of Orco+ olfactory sensory neurons in the presence of a visual target on agar. Video clips of individual D. erecta and D. melanogaster males expressing the channelrhodopsin CsChrimson under the expression of the Orco promoter in small 38-mm arenas with a small black plastic bead on the central agar patch. The representative videos show male behaviour during an initial 2-min baseline period, followed by 2 min of red LED illumination and a final 2-min period with LEDs turned off again. Displayed at 4× speed.

Group of males presented with a grid of beads. Video comparing the behaviour of five D. erecta males in a large arena with a large food patch filled with agar perfumed with ACV (orange) or an agar-only control (blue) towards a grid of small hemispherical plastic beads. Clips displayed at 10× speed.

Optogenetic activation of P1 neurons in the presence of a moving visual target. Comparison of representative video clips of D. erecta males expressing the channelrhodopsin CsChrimson in P1 neurons (using 71G01 driver) or a CsChrimson only control in a small 38-mm arena with a constantly rotating dot projected onto the floor of the arena of males. Thirty µl of either agar (blue) or agar perfumed with ACV (orange) are added to the center of the arena. Male behaviour is shown before and following onset of red LED light. Clips are shown at 2× speed.

Male courtship tracking of projected dots. Behaviour of a D. erecta male in the presence of 30 µl agar perfumed with ACV (orange) and an agar-only control (blue) towards a constantly rotating dot projected onto the surface of a small 38-mm arena. Representative videos shown at original speed.

Food-odour-dependent tracking of visual stimulus in tethered setup. Clip of a tethered D. erecta male running on a spherical treadmill presented with an oscillating ‘fictive female’ on a conical screen in front of him before and during exposure to ACV odour. For interpretability of his walking direction, the tracked movements of the treadmill are indicated as a continuous blue line. Shown at 0.5× speed.

Correlated burst of courtship activity on agar. Video clip of a group of five male and five female D. erecta in a small arena with a central food patch filled with agar showing how inactivity is interjected with a burst of spontaneous group activity. Displayed at 10× speed.

Courtship with additional moving visual stimuli. Comparison of example videos of a pair of one male and one female D. erecta in a small 38-mm arena supplemented with 30 µl agar perfumed with ACV in the center with and without two constantly rotating black dots projected onto the floor of the assay chamber. Clips played at 2× speed.

Visual social scene replay experiment. Video shows the experimental design of transforming a recording of a group of five D. erecta males and five females on ACV into a visual representation used to replay to pairs of tester males and females followed by two representative replay experiments in which D. erecta pairs are presented with 30 µl agar perfumed with ACV in the center of a 38-mm arena and either a social scene representative of a group on agar or on ACV. Behaviour clips displayed at 5× speed.

#1372. Why it's all gone wrong for Charlton: JAMES SHARPE reveals the summer failures, a player's mysterious disappearance and murmurs of yet another sale as Nathan Jones' side teeter on the brink

Published: 21:00 EDT, 6 November 2026 | Updated: 06:26 EDT, 7 November 2026

Fear is creeping back in at the Valley. Charlton’s defeat by Bolton on Tuesday night, their fourth on the bounce, was greeted with the cacophony of boos it deserved.

Eleven games without a win and teetering above the Championship relegation zone. A fanbase that has been down this long and treacherous road before, and sure as hell doesn’t want to tread it again.

Certainly not when they thought those dark days were, at last, behind them. Only 10 weeks ago, Charlton sat top of the table after victory over Preston completed a hat-trick of early season wins, including a famous triumph in front of a record Championship attendance of 62,264 at West Ham.

It was a false dawn. For the first time under Nathan Jones, the ship has stalled and, for now, is going backwards.

Charlton looked destined for relegation to League Two for the first time in their history when Jones took over in February 2024. They went 14 games unbeaten and survived. After spending eight of the previous nine seasons in the third tier, he took them up via the play-offs at the next time of asking and, last season, kept them in the Championship.

For a club that had endured so much instability, a period of normality and steady progression was on the cards. Jones is Charlton’s ninth managerial appointment since June 2016. Only now, the wonder is how much longer this can go on before nine becomes 10.

Fear is creeping back in at the Valley with Charlton 11 games without a win and teetering on the brink of the Championship relegation zone

For the first time under Nathan Jones, the ship has stalled and, for now, is going backwards

‘If I hadn’t done what I’ve done at this football club, it would have been an easier decision for them (the owners),’ Jones told South London Sport this week. ‘I have to win football games. Win games or you don’t survive.’

His next chance is against ninth-placed Sheffield United this Saturday afternoon. Jones insists he maintains a strong relationship with the Charlton board. The new chief executive Ben Mansford – formerly of Leeds, Blackpool and Barnsley and who ended the club’s spell of 19 months without one – twice tried to hire Jones at his previous clubs. Jones is understood still to have the backing of his players.

Perhaps it’s not best to let him know that both Alan Pardew and Chris Powell lost their jobs after defeats by the Blades.

‘We've spent a lot of time in League One recently and I think there is a kind of head-in-hands worry at the moment: please let's not go back there again,’ Heather McKinlay, chair of the Charlton Athletic Supporters' Trust tells Daily Mail Sport.

‘At the moment, it feels more like duty than fun. I think we have become a little bit worn down because we've been through the mill so much with the changes of ownership and the shenanigans over the near 20 years since we were in the Premier League.’

They have been through the mill, much of the difficulties driven by those in charge. Former owner Roland Duchatelet, who still owns the Valley and the training ground, once accused fans of wanting the club to fail. Charlton’s fans responded to his comments and mismanagement by carrying a red coffin to the Valley followed by a crowd of mourners in a mock funeral protest against his ownership.

They lobbed hundreds of plastic pigs on the pitch for one game, beach balls to halt another, and sent a black cab to Belgium as a ’Taxi for Roland’.

Within weeks of Duchatelet selling Charlton to businessmen Tahnoon Nimer and Matt Southall for £1, the two new men were embroiled in a bitter public row. Nimer accused Southall of using club money to fund his own lifestyle, which he denied, including renting a £150,000-a-year flat in London and giving a fleet of Range Rovers to his associates. Charlton fans occupied the boardroom in protest. Thomas Sandgaard, the next owner, was arrested by the FBI this year and charged with fraud. He denies any wrongdoing.

The highly impressive win away to West Ham in August now appears to have been a false dawn

Jones is Charlton's ninth manager in the last 10 years - but how long can he keep this up?

‘Charlton fans are a proactive lot,’ adds McKinlay. ‘If they feel they can make a difference, they’ll do something. I don’t feel we can do anything right now other than cheer them on. I think the ownership want the club to succeed. The manager wants the club to succeed. The players want the club to succeed. There's not really a baddie in this.’

As one club insider put it this week, it’s nice, in a strange way, that football is the main issue for once and not what’s going on off the field.

There is still a sense of that, mind. The current ownership group known as Global Football Partners is made up of seven shareholders, each with more than five per cent, but it remains unclear who is the driving force. Sources suggest some are more willing than others to put their money in with murmurings that the club is once again up for sale. Charlton insist they are merely looking for more investment to help drive the club forward.

Poor recruitment has not helped matters either. All the talk in the summer was about ‘evolving’ from a team that could get out of League One, then stay in the Championship, to one that could compete.

The club, however, spent a net total of just £1.5million this summer. They failed to find the right winger they needed, as a deal for Crystal Palace winger Jesurun Rak-Sakyi collapsed late on. Instead they signed teenager Junior Nkeng, who hasn’t played a single minute. A lack of creative midfielder is glaring too.

As for those who did arrive, Millenic Alli infuriated supporters in the defeat by Bolton when he headed the ball blindly into no man’s land during stoppage time with the team desperately searching for an equaliser. Nathaniel Chalobah arrived as a free agent from Sheffield Wednesday with a reputation for being injury prone. He showed his class at the start of the season, got injured, returned and is now injured again.

That’s not to mention the bizarre mystery surrounding midfielder Timothy Ouma. The Kenya international, on loan from Slavia Prague, went off to play for his country during the recent break and has not been seen since. Ouma, who has not featured in a single matchday squad since the break, has previous for this, having also failed to return after international duty while on loan at Lech Poznan.

When Jones was asked about it a few weeks ago, he responded by saying: ‘We will address those rumours when they become relevant. Anything we need to put out, we will put out.’

Kenyan midfielder Timothy Ouma went off to play for his country during the recent break and has not been seen since

Nathaniel Chalobah (right) arrived as a free agent from Sheffield Wednesday with a reputation for being injury prone. He got injured, returned and is now injured again

Charlton remain tight-lipped on whether Ouma is still absent, though one insider admitted they still hadn’t seen him since the players returned from international duty. The Kenyan FA did not respond to requests for clarification.

It makes the decision to part ways with club captain Greg Docherty in the summer look even more misguided, with this a team lacking in leadership. Jones has been left to throw all the pieces up in the air and see where they land with constant changes to the team and the line-up. Selection and formation roulette, as some are calling it.

The Welshman is not everyone’s cup of tea, frequently mocked for his David Brent style, but there’s still a belief, not least from himself, that he can turn things around. ‘He’s a maverick, but he’s our maverick,’ laughs McKinlay.

Time is running out, though, because if Charlton cannot find their way again, the alternative is already too unnerving to think about.

#1371. Arsenal late show keeps heat on Man City

This season’s Premier League title race may be locked in a paralysed state of uncertainty but Arsenal, the defending champions, are determined to keep it interesting.

While the painful delay on Manchester City’s battle against their guilty verdict threatens to drag deep into next year, Arsenal are remaining hot on their tails.

City’s lead at the top is back to three points but Arsenal’s win here was unlikely to have sent any shivers down the spines of Enzo Maresca and his players in this phoney mess of a season.

It was not until the 80th minute that Arsenal finally registered their first shot on target, and that was the moment which ended their cycle of frustration at the City Ground.

Just when it appeared Mikel Arteta was heading for a third successive goalless draw at the home of Nottingham Forest, substitute Noni Madueke’s deflected strike proved the difference.

Noni Madueke breaks the deadlock at the City Ground! 🔓 https://t.co/RdL48f3OLC

Trips to the City Ground have rarely been easy for Arsenal, with an FA Cup defeat in January 2022, at a time when Forest were still in the Championship, sparking a famous Arteta rant in the dressing room which was included in the All Or Nothing documentary.

They were far from fluent here and have now failed to score in the first half of their last six Premier League and Champions League matches.

Eberechi Eze endured a particularly difficult afternoon in what was a missed opportunity for the England international, with Madueke replacing him at half-time. Yet Arteta will argue that finding a way to win games when not at their best is a sign of champions.

“We have played 11 competitive matches and won 10 of them, we are in a good place and will improve,” Arteta said. “Since losing at Brighton we have won three games in a row so that is the response that I want.

“The level of the league has gone up again and there will be more and more surprises. We have to go again at Bayern Munich this week [in the Champions League on Wednesday night] and we will have to adapt to that one too.

“I have a smile on my face as Noni is a special guy. He’s in a good moment and after the [international] break he’s shown another level. The team needs him and he’s doing well.”

Arsenal often struggled against teams who operate with a compact midfield and defend deeply last season and this was another case in point.

When Declan Rice wastefully lifted a shot over the crossbar 18 minutes from the end, after a rare opening in the Forest area, it did appear that another draw was inevitable.

Declan Rice can't hit the target! ❌ https://t.co/kZv0k0MluO

Yet Madueke provided the crucial contribution, driving a right-footed shot towards goal which took a heavy deflection off Forest defender Jair Cunha to beat Matz Sels.

Madueke has struggled for consistency and minutes since his £52m move from Chelsea, so this felt like a big moment for the winger.

“If you look at the quality of our starting XI and bench it’s absurd,” Madueke said. “We have elite players of the highest level and it’s great to have that type of competition. You know on the bench that you’re ready to have an impact. We showed grit and determination and showed a champion spirit.”

Forest’s problems at home are increasing and Oliver Glasner is now the club’s fifth manager in a year to experience such problems. His team have now gone almost eight and a half hours without scoring in front of their own supporters. They have only recorded two home wins in the league over the past 11 months which, quite frankly, is relegation form.

They did not deserve to lose this match. Without their injured talisman Morgan Gibbs-White, Forest defended resolutely and in the second half displayed far more attacking impetus without ever truly testing Arsenal goalkeeper David Raya.

Liam Delap, their £50m record signing, produced a fine centre-forward performance and never allowed Arsenal’s centre-backs Ezri Konsa and Gabriel to feel comfortable. Goals, however, continue to elude this team.

Murillo had Forest’s best opportunity two minutes into injury time after cutting inside the penalty area but could not find the top corner.

"That was magic!" What a goal this would have been from Murillo?! 😩 https://t.co/D07lB7hN47

Another defeat will only add to their concerns and Glasner needs to quickly find a solution or face another relegation battle.

It does not promise to get easier immediately, either, with Manchester City, Chelsea and Brighton up next in the league at home, but there were encouraging signs here, despite the club sitting in the bottom three.

Glasner said: “I feel really sorry for the players because we didn’t deserve that.

“It feels unfair but I don’t want to be complaining as we are the only ones who can change it.

“It is a tough moment and we need to stick together and stay positive. Sometimes it takes a while – during my first year at Palace we didn’t start well but we had a turnaround.

“We are playing better right now but we also concede how competitive the Premier League is because every mistake you get punished.”

We knew the margins would be really small. They are extremely well coached and organised. The longer the game goes on they gain more belief. We had to be so patient - and clinical when we got the chance. The way they were defending, they were more comfortable. But we have players with different qualities and can adapt to what the game is delivering.

We have another three big chances that should be goals. That is the difference, you have to be clinical. If we keep generating them, they will come.

Let’s enjoy the win, because it was a very tough one. And then, on Wednesday, we have an incredible game against Bayern Munich away [in the Champions League].

When you see their goal it’s deflected otherwise, it’s straight to the gloves of Matz Sels. You have periods in football where you feel everything going against you and then there are periods when things are on your side.

Now it is how we deal with the situation and react as a team and just how we can change this is by staying positive, sticking together and working hard.

And having this coolness, not to worry too much because I can see good performances and not good results. The results will come if the performances stay good.

Noni [Madueke], Jurrien [Timber], Mikel [Merino] was brilliant when he came on and Viktor [Gyokeres] really changed the game - all of them did and that’s what we need. Noni obviously the highlight because he scored the goal and that’s the difference.

Sometimes you can get frustrated with teams who are difficult to break down. First half we didn’t have a shot on target and that’s something we discussed. We had another two big ones in the second half but the only one on target we had was a little deflection and it’s in.

Great reaction [after scoring goal], to have the will to defend a really open and difficult and stressful situation.

We knew it would be a tough game, it always is against Arsenal. They have a good team. But we feel we can change the result, maybe a draw, maybe a win. Now we have to put it in the past and focus on the next match.

We have a good manager and I think we are still getting his ideas. We changed everything in our system this season. It is difficult but after three or four months we keep improving and I think we are close to reaching our best.

If you look at the quality of our starting XI and bench it’s absurd so we know that we’re going to start some and finish some and for me it’s the same mentality every time I just want to create or score.

Amazing feeling [to score] but I feel better about the win.

We have elite players, all 20-something players are elite and of the highest level. Great to have that type of competition. You know on the bench you’re ready to have an impact.

32 - Since Mikel Arteta became Arsenal manager in December 2019, they have had the joint-most 1-0 wins in the Premier League of any side (32, level with Everton). Stereotype. https://t.co/nD7C3j7Xjw

Arsenal dig out a very ugly victory, and one they probably did not warrant. A draw would have been the fairest outcome from a game that was low on quality, but Arsenal’s bench makes a difference again with Noni Madueke scoring the winning goal. Forest can take positives from their performance, primarily the solidity of their defending and a more threatening Delap performance.

Forest with another late moment of danger! Delap peeled in behind the Arsenal defence, and he was found by a glorious pass, but Konsa made a fantastic last-ditch challenge to surely preserve the points from Arsenal.

What a goal that would have been from Murillo! The burly defender did so well to skip between Konsa and Saka, before sending Rice the wrong way in the box with a roll of the studs. Murillo tired for the curler into the top corner with his weaker right foot, and he was not far away. Great effort.

Arsenal have a throw in the Forest half after some grafting by Gyokeres and there are just three added minutes to play.

Hudson-Odoi carried the ball to the edge of the box and picked out Wood with a pass, but the big striker wanted too much time and Rice recovered to block.

Anything can happen when there is a one-goal margin, but Arsenal have been in complete control since scoring. Forest have lost some of their structure as they chase the game and they are more open as a result. Merino wins a free-kick, and then Gabriel ushers the ball out for a throw in.

Forest cling on by their fingernails with Arsenal flooding forward, but Merino’s pass to Saka in the box was underhit. Chris Wood and Hudson-Odoi are now on for Forest as they chase an equaliser. Cunha and McAtee the Forest players to depart.

Noni Madueke breaks the deadlock at the City Ground! 🔓 https://t.co/RdL48f3OLC

Saka floats in a teasing cross which bounces through to Sels, but that was a better Arsenal delivery. One or two signs that Timber, and his combination with Saka and Odegaard, might be the route to a goal.

Odegaard with a week free-kick from a good crossing position after Saka won a foul, before Raya’s long ball towards Gyokeres is too strong and Forest have a goal kick. Arsenal still to muster a shot on target from 73 per cent possession.

Ndoye are Dominguez are the Forest players coming off in a double change, replaced by Kalimuendo and Sangare. Forest will be worth a point if the game continues this way.

Declan Rice with a shank out for a throw when he was looking for Saka. Kalimuendo is ready to come for Forest, so Glasner is introducing another forward.

Delap with a tame shot from distance, before Timber instigates a more dangerous Arsenal attack with a reverse pass into Odegaard. The ball is worked to Madueke and his deflected cross is headed away. Arsenal building some pressure, and they have another corner. Arteta signalling that he wants to make the change before the corner is taken and here come the changes: White for Timber, Havertz for Gyokeres and Merino on for Bruno Guimaraes.

Gabriel meets Rice’s delivery, but he fails to direct his header on target.

Timber, Merino and Gyokeres are all ready to come on for Arsenal.

The game is see-sawing, Arsenal have a corner after Calafiori fed Madueke down the left and his cross was blocked. Sels punches away, and then Odegaard loses some patience and tries to find Calafiori with a pass that is not on.

Saka and Rice lose duels when fishing for fouls and Forest have another corner. Arsenal’s performance level has certainly not improved since half-time.

Arsenal clear, but Odegaard blocks a cross and Forest win a second corner in quick succession. Excellent goalkeeping from Raya to claim, and he bowls the ball forward quickly, but Forest snuff out the danger against Madueke.

The first half was an attack against defence session for long periods but Arsenal know they are in an arm wrestle now. Forest far more aggressive, and the crowd are more involved. But that could open up avenues of space. White with a really poor pass towards Saka which is astray.

Arsenal have a corner of their own after breaking from Raya’s gloves. Much more open game so far.

Forest deal with Saka’s delivery, and there was a very brief VAR check for a handball penalty. Nothing doing.

Madueke looking dangerous, receiving a Gabriel ball over the top and dashing inside but his shot was blocked.

Delap’s shot from a tight angle is then deflected wide. Forest corner, from which Murillo’s header loops into Raya’s gloves. Forest showing more attacking ambition.

Frustrating first half for Arsenal and Mikel Arteta will be demanding more from his attacking players.

Forest look relatively comfortable and had the best chance of the half with a shot from Dan Ndoye which was saved by David Raya.

Are we heading for a hat-trick of 0-0 draws at the City Ground between these two teams?

A very uneventful 45 minutes which has been played at the pace of a pre-season game at times. Similarities with the last two fixtures between these teams at the City Ground, and Arsenal’s games against Leeds and Lille this week. They put their foot on the pedal after half-time in both games, and they need to do the same here.

Guimaraes is off the pitch, and there will be more than two minutes added now as a result of his treatment. Forest win a corner, but Havertz heads away at the near post.

Just the two minutes of added time to play.

Liam Delap wins a free-kick in a shooting position for Forest after Arsenal were caught with numbers forward. Big moment for the home team, this. Calafiori was caught on the ball again, he has not had the best of games.

Glasner and Arteta dish out some instruction while there is a stoppage in play to deal with a hand in the face that troubled Schlager. Can either side find a breakthrough before the break?

David Raya claimed that Forest corner with ease and the game has now resumed its pattern. Forest retreating into their shape, and Arsenal passing in front of them. Schlager penalised for a foul on Saka, the home fans not happy with the decision, I think because Saka was going away from goal.

Rice clips in a menacing delivery, but Havertz skewed his header wide from seven or eight yards. Good chance, Arsenal’s best so far.

Arsenal work the ball across their midfield with Guimaraes, Rice and Odegaard all involved, and a dangerous Saka cross is headed behind for a corner.

Scramble! The near-post flick on caused chaos and Konsa’s goal-bound backheel was blocked, but the ball would not quite drop for Ben White to score a tap-in.

It’s a very tight affair with Arsenal enjoying more of the possession but Forest seemingly happy with that and content to them on the break.

Bruno Guimaraes has made a bright start for the visitors.

Forest’s best attacking moment of the game and it comes from an Arsenal mistake.

Saka produces his first successful dribble to beat Williams, and the left wing-back trips him at the expense of a free-kick and a booking. Rice’s delivery from the right was uncharacteristically poor.

Munoz tries to drag Forest up the pitch to apply some pressure on Arsenal but he is penalised for a shirt pull on Gabriel. The atmosphere sounds pretty sleepy, a result of some tepid Arsenal possession and Forest’s bad home record.

Forest making sure they have numbers around Saka whenever Arsenal funnel attacks down their right, which is almost always their preferred side.

Neat from Guimaraes in midfield to turn and find Saka with some earlier service, and Sels tips his cross away from danger.

Delap and Ndoye waiting for a slip-up or counter-attack but they are feeding on scraps at the moment. Arsenal yet to carve out a proper chance, though.

It’s already pretty clear that one of the key duels today will be between Gabriel and Liam Delap.

Forest’s record signing Delap has already let Gabriel know he’s in the game with his physicality.

Cute pass from Bruno Guimaraes to break the Forest midfield line and find Odegaard, but strangely the Arsenal captain could not sort his feet out to control the ball and back a clean pass. Then Williams defends well against Saka from an Arsenal attacking transition.

Pretty subdued start from Forest. The crowd’s spirits were raised there by Delap chasing down Konsa who had the deal with the sun his eyes, but the Forest striker pushed him in the back.

Arsenal enjoying all of the possession so far, and most of it has come in Forest’s half. One or two players on Arsenal’s right/Forest’s left struggling with the low evening sun. Havertz did get in behind but his cross into the middle was too strong.

Arsenal get the game under way, and play short from kick-off.

There will be a degree of pressure on birthday boy James McAtee today to make an impression.

With Morgan Gibbs-White injured, McAtee is likely to take the No 10 position and continue his redemption arc.

McAtee has been revitalised since the arrival of Oliver Glasner and this is a big afternoon for the former England under 21 international.

In honour of nine-year-old Forest fan James Kerry, who died earlier this month of cancer.

We'll wear black armbands this afternoon, as we join our hosts in remembering nine-year-old Nottingham Forest supporter, James Kerry, who passed away earlier this month following a brave battle with cancer. Rest in peace, James ❤️ https://t.co/YFIXnCfJJX

Surely we cannot have another 0-0 in this fixture? Looking at the talent in Arsenal’s front third, and the fact they are playing their two most offensive full-backs, this might be more open than assummed.

Arsenal can cut Manchester City’s lead to three points with a win today but does it all matter?

Manchester City’s battle against their guilty verdict is threatening to run into next year and this title race feels fake and damaged.

It is a sham of a season with the prospect of asterisks all over the Premier League campaign.

Arsenal can only carry on as normal as they defend their title but this is an unsatisfactory mess.

The margins are really small and it’s a team and a manager that we know really well, extraordinary manager, really well organised.

They are dangerous in many areas, a very well set-up team and you need to be very tight, very neat, very efficient in everything that you do. You have to insist and insist, and then there’s a lot of volume of actions.

[On coming from behind] Yes, and it’s part of the game, your capacity when something doesn’t go as planned to react and still win the game, and we know the challenge that we have here. In the last two years, we haven’t been able to win here and that’s an opportunity as well to show what we are made of.

Another reason Arsenal will be feeling confident today is Forest’s abysmal home form in the Premier League.

It may surprise neutrals outside of Nottingham but results at the City Ground have been poor for some time.

Indeed, it is just two league wins in 11 months in front of their own supporters which, quite frankly, is relegation form.

Before this game, Forest’s head coach Oliver Glasner said: “We have to change it. I spoke to one or two experienced lads who know Forest better than I do and talked about the situation. But if you always talk about the problem it makes it bigger and bigger.

“We haven’t scored a goal at home yet or won a game at home, and that is what we have to change.”

Trips to the City Ground have seldom been easy for Mikel Arteta, with two successive 0-0 draws in the Premier League.

An FA Cup defeat in Jan 2022, at a time when Forest were still in the Championship, sparked a famous Arteta rant in the dressing room which was included in the All Or Nothing documentary.

Yet Arsenal have secured two wins in a row since that defeat at Brighton, without being truly at their fluent best, and will be confident against a Forest team without injured talisman Morgan Gibbs-White.

Dominguez and Schlager are the preferred midfield pair in the 3-4-2-1 with Sangare on the bench. McAtee and Ndoye will support Liam Delap in attack. Much attacking responsibility on Munoz at right wing-back, who also has the cavalier Calafiori on his side of the pitch, which could prove fireworks.

Forest XI: Sels, Jair Cunha, Diomande, Murillo, Munoz, Schlager, Dominguez, Williams, McAtee, Ndoye, Delap

Subs: John Victor, Sangare, Hudson-Odoi, Wood, Kalimuendo, Yates, Netz, Milenkovic, Aina

No surprise that Havertz, Odegaard, Saka and Calafiori are restored to Arsenal’s Premier League starting XI having started on the bench in mid-week. Eze over Madueke and Guimaraes over Lewis-Skelly were closer calls for Arteta. Ben White comes in for Timber, with Arsenal managing the minutes of both right-backs.

Arsenal XI: Raya; White, Konsa, Gabriel, Calafiori; Rice, Guimaraes, Odegaard; Saka, Havertz, Eze

Subs: Meslier, Mosquera, Timber, Gyokeres, Madueke, Merino, Zubimendi, Lewis-Skelly, Dowman

🟡 𝗧𝗘𝗔𝗠𝙉𝙀𝙒𝙎 🔵 Your Sunday starters 👊 🤝 Presented by @deel

Fascinating stuff from Sam Dean this morning, who has profiled a member of Mikel Arteta’s inner circle who is not listed on Arsenal’s website. Germán Castaños, an expert in innovation who has written multiple books on alternative thinking, has become a key member of the team. Things started with a phone call with Nicolas Jover, then a meeting with Arteta and now he splits his time between Argentina and London. Find out more about Arsenal’s mystery man and his methods here.

In the ordinary course of a Premier League season, you would say Manchester City have applied pressure on Arsenal by opening up a six-point lead before the champions play at Nottingham Forest this afternoon.

This is not a normal Premier League season though, and we await to discover if the top of the league table is simply a mirage.

Regardless, Mikel Arteta and his Arsenal players have their own motivations to accumulate as many points as possible before January as they seek to retain the title for the first time since the 1930s.

Arsenal have struggled at the City Ground, drawing 0-0 on their last two Premier League visits. They also lost at Forest in May 2023, a result which confirmed Manchester City as champions at Arsenal’s expense, and were knocked out of the FA Cup by Forest in January 2022.

Forest are yet to score a home league goal under Oliver Glasner, another data point suggesting this will be a low-scoring game.

That might not be the full story though, with Forest creating a hatful of chances in their defeat at Crystal Palace last week and Arsenal also playing a more inventive, technical game with the ball so far this season.

Arsenal have yet to score from a non-penalty set-piece, and their percentage of goals from open play is now the highest in the Premier League.

Morgan Gibbs-White is a doubt after sustaining what Glasner described as a “minor muscle injury” at Palace and his involvement in the game will be a last-minute call. With the exception of Christos Tzolis, Piero Hincapie and long-term absentee William Saliba, Arsenal’s squad is in pretty good health. Bukayo Saka, Martin Odegaard, Kai Havertz, Riccardo Calafiori and Ben White could be recalled to Arteta’s starting XI after starting the Champions League win over Lille on the bench.

#1369. Derided Thierno Barry is no longer a source of frustration as star fires Everton to victory over Coventry on another big night for David Moyes amid Jack Grealish drama

Published: 17:29 EDT, 6 November 2026 | Updated: 06:27 EDT, 7 November 2026

Maybe Everton should request to play under the lights every week. It certainly seems to push David Moyes' team to new heights.

Following hot on the heels of consecutive night victories over Newcastle United, Friday's 3-1 win against Coventry City was a reminder of why, under Moyes, there is renewed sense of optimism at Everton.

Up to fifth, above Liverpool, and in a Carabao Cup quarter-final at Fleetwood, it could prove to be a special season.

This always felt like a big task for Frank Lampard, back at Everton for the first time since his sacking in 2023.

Popular as the ex-manager may be, there's no room for sentiment, certainly not from Moyes on a night he took charge of his 592nd game, drawing level with Harry Catterick for managing the most games in the club's history.

He'll set it outright after the international break against Brentford and Keith Andrews, who was 21 when Moyes first took up the reins at Everton.

Thierno Barry (right) now has 10 goals this season after being widely derided in his first season on Merseyside

Kiernan Dewsbury-Hall had been left out of the England squad in the morning, but refused to let it spoil his night

His side started impressively, fashioning three shots in the opening 10 minutes, before losing all momentum and allowing Coventry into proceedings.

It took going 1-0 down, to a soft Yann Gboho goal, for the hosts to come alive. Thierno Barry, so often the source of frustration last season, was magnificent and all but won the game with a five-minute brace in the second half.

The striker didn't score his first goal until December last season. This campaign, he's reached 10 before the second international break. Moyes joked post-match that Erling Haaland should watch his back in the Golden Boot race is starting to feel less absurd. Barry now sits joint second in the charts.

Both goals against Coventry came via back post-duels. The first he confidently headed past Carl Rushworth, before bundling in a second five minutes later.

The disgruntled home fans booed the team off at half-time, yet were jubilantly cheering and signing after Barry's brace. The Frenchman danced on the pitch at full-time and was serenaded by the South Stand.

'I don't see loads of young centre-forwards scoring loads of goals in the Premier League,' said Moyes.

'He's come in and has settled in a bit more. His language and communication is better and obviously he's worked to get himself into the positions to score.'

Barry wasn't the only Everton goalscorer, of course. Kiernan Dewsbury-Hall was not one of the three Everton players named in Thomas Tuchel's England squad on Friday - only Arsenal had more representatives.

EVERTON (4-2-3-1): Pickford 5; Rohl 5 (O'Brien 73min, 6), Tarkowski 5, Branthwaite 6 (Keane 89), Mykolenko 6; Armstrong 6 (Hackney 73, 6), Garner 6; Dibling 5 (Johnson 73, 5), DEWSBURY-HALL 8, George 5 (Alcaraz 90); Barry 8.

COVENTRY CITY (4-2-3-1): Rushworth 4; van Ewijk 5, Mfuni 6, Pinnock 6, Dasilva 6; Yirenkyi 6, Torp 6 (Grimes 86); Sakamoto 5 (Tchaouna 86), Rudoni 5 (Hamer 86), Gboho 6 (Thomas-Asante 73, 5); Awoniyi 5 (Cherif 87).

But the midfielder sent a pointed message to the Three Lions' boss with a superb showing that was capped with a late powerful goal to end the contest.

'It was a disappointing morning, I'm not going to lie,' Dewsbury-Hall told Sky Sports after the game. 'It's a massive dream to play for my country. I know I was close.

'Yeah, sad, but really proud of myself and how I have reacted. All I can keep doing is putting in good performances and hopefully one day I get the nod, because I'm never going to give up. I've got the mentality. I'll keep pushing and pushing and see what happens.'

'He's desperate to play for England,' added Moyes. 'You never know if England get a couple of injuries, or anything changes.'

What ended as a comfortable win could have been a different outcome had Jame Tarkowski been punished for a hair pull on Caleb Yirenkyi, or if Vitalii Mykolenko's tussle with Taiwo Awoniyi in the box had been deemed a foul.

Both were checked and cleared by VAR, as was a handball claim in the build-up to Barry's second goal.

'Tarky pulls on Caleb's hair, they [VAR] are saying it's not enough of a pull,' said an aggrieved Lampard afterwards. 'That's a hard area to be in. What is hair pull and what's not?

'I think Taiwo, on the edge of the box was a penalty. I feel there's a penalty by the time Myko's knee is in the back of Taiwo's knee on the line of the box.

'Then the Barry one is handball. He flicks it in [with the hand] with the final touch. Nothing went for us tonight.'

#1368. Observation of prethermal dynamical phase transitions and resonant melting

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Nature (2026) Cite this article

The dynamics of isolated quantum systems following a sudden quench has a central role in many areas of material science, high-energy physics and quantum chemistry1,2,3,4. Such far-from-equilibrium quantum dynamics—which features complex phenomena with implications for thermalization, non-equilibrium phase transitions and Floquet phase engineering5,6,7,8—is challenging to study numerically, in particular, in high-dimensional systems9,10. Here we use a programmable neutral-atom quantum simulator11 to systematically explore quench dynamics in spin models with up to 180 qubits. By initializing the system in a product state and performing quenches across a broad parameter space, we discover several stable, qualitatively distinct dynamical regimes. We trace their robustness to Floquet-like prethermal steady states8 that are stabilized over exponentially long emergent timescales by strong dynamical constraints. We further observe sharp peaks in the dynamical response that are quantitatively explained by the structured melting of prethermalization through resonances. In two dimensions, we uncover a prethermally driven, first-order dynamical phase transition linked to the proliferation of Néel-order defects6,12, and probe it quantitatively using a generalized Clausius–Clapeyron test. Together, these results establish a programmable route to high-energy prethermal phase structure: long-lived dynamical phases, their resonant breakdown and a first-order dynamical phase transition that is not inherited from the equilibrium phase boundaries.

Numerical simulations for a 1D chain of N = 16 atoms with periodic boundary conditions and Rb/a = 1.4. a,b. Simulations including the full experimentally relevant noise model. a. Time evolution of \(\langle {\hat{O}}_{ZZ}\rangle \) at Δ/Ω = 0.2 and 3.7. Solid curves show noisy numerics including readout confusion; shaded regions indicate the total 1σ uncertainty obtained by combining trajectory and shot-noise errors in quadrature. Noiseless numerics and experimental data are shown for comparison. b. Time-averaged \(\langle {\hat{O}}_{ZZ}\rangle \) versus detuning, averaged over 0≤t≤4 μs; shading indicates the corresponding total 1σ uncertainty. The noisy numerics use the Aquila-relevant noise model of Extended Data Table 1, with 20 stochastic trajectories, 120 shots per time point, and a sampling interval of 0.01 μs. c,d. Simulations including only positional atom disorder. c. Increase of the resonance peak width near Δ/Ω ≈ 3.7, relative to the zero-disorder case, as a function of the positional disorder strength σp, extracted from Lorentzian fits, together with a simple classical estimate. d. Time-averaged \(\langle {\hat{O}}_{ZZ}\rangle \) versus detuning for several values of σp. Increasing positional disorder selectively broadens and smooths the resonance peaks, while leaving the rest of the long-time response comparatively unchanged under experimentally relevant noise.

Experimental results for 180 atoms on the cut Rb/a = 1.4. a. The time-averaged expectation values of several k-island observables, namely the xyd 1-island observable and the xy k-island observable for k = 1, 2, 3, over time intervals with (top) different initial times ti and fixed final time tf = 4.0 μs, and (bottom) fixed initial time ti = 0.8 μs and different final times tf. The grey dashed vertical lines mark the quench parameters of the time series in panel b, namely the peaks of each island operator (Δ/Ω = 0.0, 1.2, 3.6, 4.8) and the point close to the right exit of the xy 1-island operator region (Δ/Ω = 2.0). b. The time evolution of the expectation values of the xyd 1-island observable and the xy k-island observable with k = 1, 2, 3. The drawing on the right shows an example of island conversion processes possible in the 2D system (equivalent to the 1D island conversion Hamiltonian discussed in the Supplementary Information). The arrows in the panels indicate the time series segments for the main resonance at Δ/Ω = 3.6 that tentatively reveal island conversion dynamics: two-islands are rapidly created and then slowly converted into a mix of one- and three-islands. The experimental data shown are derived from 100 samples per time evolution, with error bars denoting one standard deviation across the samples.

a. The time-averaged expectation values of the island operator sum on the cut Rb/a = 1.4 for 16 atoms, and the thermal expectation values of the observable for the effective temperature of the quench using the nearest-neighbor blockade subspace (thermal xy blockade) and the full Hilbert space (thermal full). b. The dependence of the time-averaged blockade violation density \({\hat{O}}_{nn}^{(1)}\) (also shown in Extended Data Fig. 6a) on V1/Ω at representative constant detuning cuts for 144 atoms. To normalize the blockade violation density to the connectivity and boundary conditions, we scale it by N/NB, where NB = 2NxNy − Nx − Ny is the number of nearest-neighbor bonds. The states along these cuts are prethermal, and thus over a fixed time interval the time averages after peak exhibit exponential scaling [equation (22)], as evidenced by the dashed lines showing fits \(\propto {e}^{-c({V}_{1}/\varOmega )}\). As shown in the Supplementary Information, the upward curvature observed in the experiments relative to the clean exponential scalings at large V1/Ω can be explained by the position disorder, while the calibrated readout errors set the final saturation floor. The experimental data shown are derived from 100 samples per time evolution, with error bars denoting one standard deviation across the samples.

a. The dependence of Δc/Ω (as extracted from \(\overline{\langle {\hat{O}}_{L}^{(1)}\rangle }\) using the procedure described in Methods) on inverse linear system size for Rb/a = 1.4 cut. The classical prediction, given by Δc/V2 = 2 − 2(1/Nx + 1/Ny) + 2/(NxNy), is shown for comparison. b. The dependence of the conjugate variable jump ratio (\({\delta }_{c}\overline{\langle {\sum }_{i}{\hat{n}}_{i}\rangle }/{\delta }_{c}\overline{\langle {\sum }_{i}{\hat{n}}_{i}{\hat{n}}_{\langle \langle i\rangle \rangle }\rangle }\)) on the inverse linear system size. The jump ratio is used to probe the Clausius-Clapeyron relation at the DPT. Both the transition point and the jump ratio converge as the system size increases, consistent with a first-order transition. The experimental data shown are derived from 100 samples per time evolution, with error bars denoting statistical and fitting uncertainties as described in Methods.

The classical spin dynamics model is described in the Supplementary Information, where the 2D square lattice has coordination numbers z1 = z2 = z3 = 4. a. Dynamical phase diagram in terms of the long-time averages of the (squared) spin component \({S}_{z}^{2}\). Panels b,c show the three (squared) spin components on b. the cut Rb/a = 1.4 across the phase transition and c. the cut Rb/a = 0.7 across the crossover, each indicated by a grey dashed horizontal line in panel a. The black dashed lines in panels a,b show the phase transition from the approximate analytic solution of the Stoner-Wohlfarth model.

Experimental phase diagrams extended down to Rb/a = 1.0 for 144 atoms. a. The time-averaged expectation values of the Rydberg density observable \({\hat{O}}_{n}\) and the k-neighbor correlation observables \({\hat{O}}_{nn}^{(k)}\) for k = 1, 2 (defined in the main text). Besides the crossover, at low Rb and Δ ≈ 2V1 we observe another distinct dynamical regime, which corresponds to antiblockade dynamics73 characterized by expanding excitation loops74. b. The time-averaged expectation values of the xyk-island observables \({\hat{O}}_{L}^{(k)}\) for k = 1, 2, 3 (equation (4) and surrounding text). The atom schematics in the upper corners show the types and sizes of Rydberg excitations that the observables measure. The grey horizontal line indicates the lower bound Rb/a = 1.2 of the phase diagrams for 180 atoms shown in Fig. 4a. The first-order DPT smooths to a crossover at low Rb, in analogy with the classical Stoner-Wohlfarth scenario (Extended Data Fig. 5). The experimental data shown are derived from 100 samples per time evolution, with error bars denoting one standard deviation across the samples.

The lattices are shown for Rb/a = 1.4. 1D lattice with a. 52 atoms; and b. 16 atoms, where the field of view can accommodate 2 parallel copies with separation b = 5a. 2D square lattice with c. 180 atoms; and d. 16 atoms, where the field of view can accommodate 6 parallel copies with separation b = 5a. e. Pulse sequences. (Top) The Rabi frequency Ω is set to a constant value Ω/2π = 2.5 MHz. (Bottom) The detuning Δ is set in the range Δ/Ω ∈ [−4.0, 6.0], and shown here for Δ/Ω = 0.4.

Experimental results on the cut Rb/a = 1.4. Panels a-c show experiments with (left) N = 52 atoms and (right) N = 16 atoms. The geometries are shown in Extended Data Fig. 7. a. The time-averaged expectation values of the \({\hat{O}}_{nn}\) observables and the k-island observables \({\hat{O}}_{L}^{(k)}\) for k = 1, 2, 3. Experimental \({\hat{O}}_{L}^{(k)}\) data is equivalent to Fig. 3b. b. The time evolution of the expectation value of the 1-island observable for several values of Δ/Ω on the right exit from the central region, shown as dotted vertical lines in a. c. The time-average \(\bar{p}(\alpha | \varDelta /\varOmega )=\frac{1}{T}{\sum }_{i}p(\alpha | \varDelta /\varOmega ,{t}_{i})\) of the Hamming weight probability distribution \(p(\alpha | \varDelta /\varOmega ,t)={\rm{Tr}}\,(\rho (t){\hat{P}}_{\alpha })\). Projectors \({\hat{P}}_{\alpha }\) arise from the spectral decomposition of the (unnormalized) Hamming weight operator \({\hat{Q}}_{n}\equiv N{\hat{O}}_{n}={\sum }_{\alpha }{\lambda }_{\alpha }{\hat{P}}_{\alpha }\), where λα = 0, …, N denote the possible Hamming weights. The time average is equivalent to marginalization over ti with p(ti) = 1/T. The grey dashed vertical lines identify the distribution at Δ/Ω = 0. d. The mean and variance of the time-averaged Hamming weight probability distribution at Δ/Ω = 0, measured in experiments with different system sizes N. The data are linear, with fits yielding the slope of ~0.275 ± 0.002 for the mean and ~0.106 ± 0.006 for the variance, shown respectively by the red and green solid lines. The approximate scalings are 1/4 and 1/8, shown respectively by the red and green dashed lines, consistent with a state that ergodically explores the blockade subspace. e. The time-averaged Hamming weight probability from numerical simulations with 16 atoms. The experimental data shown are derived from 120 samples per time evolution for 52 atom experiments and 100 samples per time evolution for 16 atom experiments, with error bars denoting one standard deviation across the samples.

Numerical studies of multiple observables, scaling, and averaging for the 1D chain in a circular geometry on the cut Rb/a = 1.4. The time-averaged expectation values are computed as \(\overline{\langle \hat{O}\rangle }=\frac{1}{{t}_{f}}{\int }_{0}^{{t}_{f}}{\rm{d}}t\langle \hat{O}(t)\rangle \). a. The time averages of the blockade-violation density \({\hat{O}}_{nn}\) operator, the diagonal \({\hat{O}}_{ZZ}\) operator (also presented in the main text Fig. 2d), and the off-diagonal \({\hat{O}}_{XX}\) operator. The \({\hat{O}}_{nn}\) response vanishes at the main peak, but captures the resonances, suggesting their origin from blockade violations; the \({\hat{O}}_{XX}\) response showcases non-analyticities at points where the dynamics is expected to change abruptly. b. The time averages for different system sizes N = 10, …, 20 and final time tf = 10 μs. The curves are nearly identical, indicating a weak system size dependence. c. The time averages for N = 16 atoms and different final times tf. The curves rapidly converge in tf ≈ 0.5 μs. The dashed line denotes the curve for tf = 100 μs, which is the longest time examined in the numerics, while the squares denote the diagonal ensemble averages, which are equal to the time averages in the strictly infinite-time limit. d. The time averages of the blockade-violation operator for N = 16 atoms and different quench parameters Δ/Ω, reflecting the 1D experiments in Fig. 3a. Similar to the experimental results, the curves show exponential decay, corroborating prethermal dynamics even at small system sizes.

Numerical results obtained using the time-evolving block decimation (TEBD) method for a chain of N = 52 Rydberg atoms with open boundary conditions. The blockade radius is Rb/a = 1.4. The system is evolved up to \({t}_{\max }=4.0\,\mu {\rm{s}}\) with a time step Δt = 0.01 μs, and the Hamiltonian includes nearest-neighbor and next-nearest-neighbor interactions, with longer-range terms truncated. a. Real-time dynamics of \(\langle {\hat{O}}_{ZZ}\rangle \) for two representative detunings, (top) Δ/Ω = 0.0 and (bottom) Δ/Ω = 0.5, illustrating convergence of the oscillatory behavior with increasing maximum MPS bond dimension \({\chi }_{\max }\). b. Time-averaged value \(\overline{\langle {\hat{O}}_{ZZ}\rangle }\) as a function of detuning Δ/Ω, where the plotted values are averaged over the final 2.0 μs of the evolution. The curves correspond to different maximum bond dimensions \({\chi }_{\max }\). Both the real-time dynamics and the time-averaged observables exhibit rapid convergence as \({\chi }_{\max }\) increases, with \({\chi }_{\max }\gtrsim 256\) yielding nearly indistinguishable results, indicating that the dynamics are well converged with respect to entanglement truncation at the probed times.

This Supplementary Information file contains the following sections: I. Supplementary experimental data on dynamical regimes in 1D; II. Characterization of dynamical regimes in 1D; III. Perturbation theory of the resonances; IV. Characterization of dynamical regimes in 2D; V. Classical Stoner–Wohlfarth transition; and Supplementary References.
